Hold onto this word, because it returns at the end of the letter. Paul will write in chapter three that Christ will change the body of our humiliation — tapeinōsis, the noun from this verb — into the likeness of the body of His glory. He entered your low place on purpose. He will not leave you in it.
stations.live: Find the low place you have been avoiding — an apology, a menial task, a conversation that will cost you standing. Go there once this week, on purpose.

stations.verse: Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name,
stations.question: Do I actually believe that the way up, in God’s economy, runs downward?
stations.gloss: to exalt to the highest place; to raise beyond all
body: comparison PHILIPPIANS 2:9 — THE ONLY OCCURRENCE IN THE NEW TESTAMENT Hyperypsoō joins hyper, above or beyond, to hypsoō, to lift up. It occurs only here in the New Testament, though the Greek Old Testament uses it in Psalm 97:9 of the Lord exalted far above all gods. Not merely exalted — supremely exalted, raised past the point where comparison means anything.

The word answers the descent line for line. He humbled Himself to the lowest point a man can be brought; God raised Him past the highest point a name can occupy. The deeper the descent, the higher the exaltation, and Paul builds the sentence so you cannot miss the symmetry.

And mark the therefore, because a great deal of Christian living hangs on it. The exaltation is not compensation for the humiliation, as though the Father were making it up to Him. It is the Father’s verdict on it — a public declaration that this is what glory actually looks like and always did. The way up is not a different road from the way down. It is the same road, walked to the end.
stations.live: Identify one place where you are climbing. Ask what the downward version of that ambition would look like this week, and take one step of it.

practices.title: FIND THE GRIP
practices.body: Name what you are holding: seniority, being right, a reputation for competence, a role someone might take. Write down what you are afraid would happen if you opened your hand. Then read verse six again and notice who had the most to lose and held it loosest.

practices.title: REMOVE THE VISIBILITY
practices.body: Do one genuinely good thing this week with the audience deliberately removed — no mention, no report, no place where it can be noticed later. If the appeal drains out of it once nobody can see, you have found your empty glory.

practices.title: TAKE THE LOW TASK
practices.body: Pick one job that is beneath your position and do it, quietly, this week. Not as an exercise in self-abasement — as practice in a direction. He did not wait until it was safe to descend, and He is the only one who ever had a position worth protecting.

practices.title: COUNT SOMEONE BETTER
practices.body: Take one relationship where your interests and theirs are in genuine tension. Make the reckoning Paul asks for: decide, in advance, that their interest ranks above yours in this instance. You are not asked to feel small. You are asked to make a decision.

practices.title: WALK THE STEPS DOWN
practices.body: Read verses six through eight slowly, once a day, and walk the descent with Him: form of God, form of a servant, likeness of men, obedient, death, the cross. Do it until the distance He came stops being a doctrine and starts being a place you recognize — because it ends in your own dust.

title: He Emptied Himself
subtitle: from dust to the mind of Christ
keyVerse: but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men.

passage.text: If therefore there is any exhortation in Christ, if any consolation of love, if any fellowship of the Spirit, if any tender mercies and compassion,
make my joy full by being like-minded, having the same love, being of one accord, of one mind;
doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself;
each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.
Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus,
who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped,
but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men.
And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.
Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name,
that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth,
and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.

stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land first, then answer honestly.
lifeIntro: This week is about locating your grip — the thing your hand has been closed around so long you have stopped noticing — and learning the mind of a Christ who went down on purpose.
lifePulls: The one Person who could never have lost His standing is the one who declined to guard it. That is what exposes the lie in your defensiveness.
prayer: Father, show me what my hand has been closed around. Your Son had everything and clutched none of it. He emptied Himself and came down to a servant’s form, to death, to the cross. He came down farther than I have fallen. Give me His mind today, in one specific room, with one specific person. Let me count that man as more important than myself, and mean it. Open what I have been guarding, and let me spend it. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, show me what my hand has been closed around.
Your Son had everything and clutched none of it.
He emptied Himself and came down to a servant’s form, to death, to the cross.
He came down farther than I have fallen.
Give me His mind today, in one specific room, with one specific person.
Let me count that man as more important than myself, and mean it.
Open what I have been guarding, and let me spend it.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: Paul settles a quarrel in a small church by taking it to the cross. Christ did not consider equality with God a thing to be grasped; He emptied Himself, took the form of a servant, and became obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross. Therefore God highly exalted Him, and the road up is the road He walked down — as far down as you have fallen.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, off the position you have been quietly defending and onto the One who had everything and clutched none of it. You are tired in a specific way — the fatigue of a hand that has been closed for years. You may not be able to name what you are holding. You will be able to feel it the next time someone takes credit for your work and you cannot get to sleep.

Lift up your eyes to what He let go of. Existing in the form of God, showing forth all that God is, secure beyond any possibility of loss — and He did not consider equality with the Father a thing to be clutched for His own advantage. The only Person in the universe whose position was genuinely unassailable is the only one who refused to guard it. Everything you grip, you grip because you are afraid. He was not afraid, and He still let go.

Lift up your eyes and see how far down He went. Not to a lower rank, not to a humbler station — to a servant’s form, to a man’s body, to obedience, to death, and then past the ordinary dignity of dying to the death of the cross, a death of open shame. Whatever face your dust wears, He has been beneath it. There is no floor you can reach that He has not already stood on.

Lift up your eyes and hear the therefore. God highly exalted Him and gave Him the name above every name, and the exaltation was not a consolation for the descent. It was the Father’s verdict on it — this is what glory looks like, and always did. Lift your eyes off the ground you have been clinging to. The road up is the road He walked down, and He walked it as far as you.
closingVerse: but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men.
carry: What has your hand been closed around for so long that you no longer notice the grip — and what would it cost to open it in one room this week?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: There are two ditches on this road, and a man usually spends his life in one of them without ever suspecting that the other exists.

The first ditch is the grinding man. He knows that the Christian life requires effort, and he supplies it. He gets up early, keeps the list, tries harder after every failure, and cannot understand why twenty years of sincere labor have produced so little visible change. He is exhausted, and the exhaustion has a particular flavor: the fatigue of a man who suspects the whole thing depends on him and knows he is not up to it.

The second ditch is the passive man. He has learned, correctly, that he cannot sanctify himself. He has heard that striving is legalism and that the flesh profits nothing, and he has drawn the natural conclusion: wait. Let go and let God. So he waits, and nothing happens, and the sins he was told to stop fighting settle in as permanent residents. He is not exhausted. He is comfortable, which is worse.
Both men are reading the same verse and each is taking half of it.

The dust offers you a choice between a Christianity of gritted teeth and a Christianity of folded hands, and it will happily supply the verses for either. What it will not let you see is the little conjunction in the middle of Philippians 2:13, which joins the two halves into one sentence and dissolves the choice entirely. Psalm 119:25 is the prayer of a soul in one ditch or the other: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word (NKJV).

And the reviving word of Philippians 2 is this: work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you both to will and to work. Not but. For. God’s working is not the alternative to your effort. It is the reason for it.

sections.heading: A Command to a Church That Was Doing Well
pulls: Work out your own salvation — for it is God who works in you. Not ‘but.’ The conjunction is the whole Christian life, and both ditches lose it.
paras: Notice who receives this command, because it is not a congregation in crisis. So then, my beloved, even as you have always obeyed, not only in my presence, but now much more in my absence. Paul commends their obedience before he commands anything. These were not backsliders needing to be shaken. They were faithful people who had kept going when the apostle was not there to watch — which is exactly the situation in which a church is most tempted to coast.

And the so then connects it to what came before. The hymn of Christ’s descent is not a devotional interlude; it is the ground of the command. Because Christ emptied Himself and obeyed to the point of death, and because God has highly exalted Him — therefore, work out what has been worked in.

Then the phrase that has troubled sincere readers for centuries: with fear and trembling. It does not mean terror of God’s rejection; the same letter has already promised that He will complete the work. It means the seriousness appropriate to handling something of enormous weight — the attentiveness of a man carrying something he did not make and cannot replace. Paul uses the phrase elsewhere of ordinary reverence in difficult work. Sanctification is not a casual business, and a man who approaches it casually has misjudged what he is holding.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: WORK OUT, NOT WORK FOR
paras: Everything turns on a preposition here, so get it right.

Paul does not say work for your salvation. He says work out your own salvation — and the verb means to bring something to its full effect, to carry a thing through until the result is visible on the outside. You do not work for a salvation you do not have. You work out a salvation you have already been given.

The picture is of something already deposited in you being brought to expression. A mine is worked out; the gold was in the ground before anyone arrived with a pick. A problem is worked out; the answer was always implied by the terms. Paul is not asking the Philippians to earn anything. He is asking them to let what God has put in them come all the way out into their Tuesdays.

And note your own. The Greek is emphatic, and in context it is pointedly plural — a whole congregation working out together the salvation they have been given. This follows immediately on a passage about rivalry and empty glory, which means Paul is not calling them to private spiritual improvement. He is calling them to make the reality of their salvation visible in how they treat one another, especially with the apostle out of the room.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: THE FOR THAT FILLS BOTH DITCHES
paras: For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure. This is one of the most important sentences in the New Testament for ordinary Christian living, and its power is in the conjunction. If Paul had written but, the two halves would be rivals and you would have to decide how much of your sanctification is yours. He wrote for. God’s work is offered as the grounds of your effort — the reason you can afford to try.

Then look at the scope of what God works. Not only the doing, which you might have expected — He also works the willing. He is upstream of your wanting. The desire you had this morning to pray, the reluctance you overcame, the sudden unwelcome willingness to apologize: God was in the room before you were.

That is a great mercy for the grinding man, because it means his effort is not self-generated and does not have to be self-sustained. And it is a rebuke to the passive man, because the thing God works in him is willing and working — not tranquility. If God is working, something will move.

And the whole of it is for his good pleasure. Eudokia — His delight, His gracious intention. Your sanctification is not a chore God is grimly overseeing. It is something He wants, and He is doing it in you because it pleases Him to.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: WITHOUT COMPLAINING AND ARGUING
paras: Then comes the application, and it is smaller than you expect and harder than it looks.
Do all things without complaining and arguing.

After the highest Christology in Paul’s letters and the deepest statement of divine and human agency in Scripture, the practical instruction is: stop grumbling. It seems anticlimactic until you notice the echo. Complaining is the signature sin of the wilderness generation — a people rescued by sheer grace who spent forty years murmuring about the catering. Paul is quoting their world back at the Philippians, and the next verse makes it explicit: children of God without defect in the middle of a crooked and perverse generation, which is Moses’ own description of Israel, now applied to the world around the church.

The point is pointed. The redeemed community’s most characteristic failure is not scandal. It is a low, continuous murmur — a running commentary on the leadership, the hardship, the accommodations, the other people. It never rises to the level of anything a man would confess.

And Paul makes the alternative visible: among whom you are seen as lights in the world, holding up the word of life. A church that has stopped grumbling shines. Not because cheerfulness is impressive, but because in a complaining world, a community that is not complaining is inexplicable.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: POURED OUT AND GLAD
paras: The section ends with an image from the altar.
Yes, and if I am poured out on the sacrifice and service of your faith, I rejoice, and rejoice with you all.

The verb is spendō, used of the drink offering — the cup of wine poured out beside the main sacrifice, soaking into the ground and gone. Paul is contemplating his own execution, and he does not cast himself as the sacrifice. The sacrifice is your faith, the offering the Philippians are making of their own lives. Paul is only the libation poured out alongside it.

That is a hard piece of self-assessment from the apostle to the nations. He does not see his death as the main event. He sees a congregation’s faith as the offering and himself as the small cup poured out beside it — visible for a moment, then absorbed into the ground, and nobody thinks about the libation once the smoke goes up.

And his response to that prospect is I rejoice, and rejoice with you all — then he turns and commands the same of them: In the same way, you also rejoice, and rejoice with me. Four uses of joy in two verses, at the exact point where he is discussing his own death.

That is what the working-out looks like in a man who has been thoroughly worked in. Not grim endurance and not passive waiting. A poured-out life, spent gladly on other people’s faith, by a man who knows Who has been doing the work all along.

stations.verse: So then, my beloved, even as you have always obeyed, not only in my presence, but now much more in my absence, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling.
stations.question: Which ditch am I in this year — grinding as though it depended on me, or waiting as though nothing were asked?
stations.gloss: trembling, quaking, especially from fear
body: Tromos comes from tremō, to tremble. It is the body’s word for fear — the shaking of a man who knows he is standing before something larger than himself. Paul pairs it with phobos, fear, the same pair the Greek Old Testament uses for the dread that fell on the nations before Israel.

What is striking is where Paul puts it. He does not attach trembling to the fear of losing salvation. He attaches it to working it out — and then, in the next breath, gives the reason: for it is God who works in you. The trembling is not the anxiety of a man unsure whether God will finish. It is the seriousness of a man who has realized that God Himself is at work in the room.

Paul uses the same pair of himself. He came to Corinth in weakness, in fear, and in much trembling, and what followed was a demonstration of the Spirit and of power. A man who trembles before God does not have less confidence. He has stopped trusting his own.
stations.live: Name one thing God has clearly put in you that has never made it to the surface in a relationship. Work it out this week — seriously, as a man who knows God is at work in the room.

stations.verse: For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure.
stations.question: Do I believe God is upstream of my wanting — or only of my ability?
stations.gloss: good pleasure; a gracious intention freely taken up
body: Eudokia joins eu, well, to dokeō, to think or seem good. It means the settled good pleasure of someone who has chosen freely — not a duty accepted but a delight determined upon. Paul uses it in Ephesians of God predestining His people to adoption according to the good pleasure of his desire.

Here it is the motive behind God’s work inside you. He is not grimly supervising your sanctification because He said He would. The willing and the working are produced in you for his good pleasure — because it delights Him to do it.

That changes the emotional weather of the whole Christian life. If your growth is a project God has taken on reluctantly, every failure is a strain on His patience. If your growth is His eudokia, then the God who is working in you is enjoying the work — and a workman who delights in a project does not abandon it when the material is difficult.
stations.live: The next time you notice a right desire rising in you this week, stop and name its source out loud: ‘That was not mine. You were in the room first.’

stations.verse: Do all things without complaining and arguing,
stations.question: Who is the running commentary in my head usually about?
stations.gloss: a murmur; low, continuous grumbling under the
body: breath PHILIPPIANS 2:14; JOHN 7:12; 1 PETER 4:9 Gongysmos is an onomatopoeic word — it sounds like the thing it names, a low muttering. It is the standard term in the Greek Old Testament for what Israel did in the wilderness: not open rebellion, not a declaration of unbelief, but a continuous undertone of dissatisfaction from a people who had just been rescued.

Paul is deliberately putting the Philippians in that story. The very next verse calls the surrounding world a crooked and perverse generation — Moses’ phrase for Israel herself. The warning is unmistakable: a redeemed people can murmur their way through a wilderness while eating bread from heaven.

And notice that gongysmos never feels like a sin worth confessing. It is too small, too reasonable, too accurate. That is exactly what makes it the characteristic failure of the church rather than an occasional one — and why Paul, having just described the mind of Christ, aims first at the murmur.
stations.live: Go one day this week with no commentary — spoken or internal — about a person or a circumstance you did not choose. Notice what hour you fail, and what you were about to say.

stations.verse: that you may become blameless and harmless, children of God without defect in the middle of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you are seen as lights in the world,
stations.question: Am I trying to be impressive to the people around me — or simply visible?
stations.gloss: a luminary; a light-bearing body set in the heavens
body: PHILIPPIANS 2:15; REVELATION 21:11; GENESIS 1:14 (Greek OT) Phōstēr is not the ordinary word for a lamp. It is the word the Greek Old Testament uses in Genesis for the lights God set in the expanse of the heavens — sun, moon, and stars, hung in place to give light to the earth.

So Paul is not describing a church that shines brightly by effort. He is describing bodies that were placed. A star does not strain to be visible; it is what it is, set where it was set, and the darkness around it does the rest of the work.

And that is the connection to the verse before, which is otherwise puzzling. How does a congregation become luminous? By not grumbling. In a world of continuous low complaint, a community that has stopped murmuring is simply inexplicable — and the inexplicable is exactly what light is in a dark place. You are not asked to be impressive. You are asked to be set in place and not go out.
stations.live: Stop trying to be impressive in one setting this week. Just be steady, uncomplaining, and present. Let the contrast do the work a performance never could.

stations.verse: Yes, and if I am poured out on the sacrifice and service of your faith, I rejoice, and rejoice with you all.
stations.question: Could I be glad about work that will be absorbed into someone else’s life and never traced back to me?
stations.gloss: to pour out as a drink offering beside a sacrifice
body: Spendō names the libation — the cup of wine poured out at the altar alongside the principal offering, commanded in the law to accompany the burnt offering. It soaked into the ground and was gone. Nobody watched the libation; the eyes were on the sacrifice.

Paul uses the verb of his own probable execution, and the self-assessment inside it is humbling. He does not cast himself as the sacrifice. The sacrifice is the sacrifice and service of your faith — the offering these Philippians are making of their own lives. Paul is the wine poured out beside it, absorbed into the ground, unremarked.

The greatest missionary in Christian history regarded his death as the accompaniment to a small congregation’s faith. And his response to the prospect is joy, repeated twice and then commanded back: In the same way, you also rejoice, and rejoice with me. A man who has been thoroughly worked in by God can be poured out and be glad about it.
stations.live: Do something this week that will be entirely absorbed into someone else’s life — untraceable, uncredited, gone. Then see whether you can be glad about it.

practices.title: NAME YOUR DITCH
practices.body: Write down honestly which error is yours this year: effort without dependence, or dependence without effort. Most men can name it in one sentence if they stop defending it. Then read Philippians 2:12–13 aloud as a single sentence, with the for emphasized, and notice which half you have been skipping.

practices.title: WORK ONE THING ALL THE WAY OUT
practices.body: Identify something God has genuinely put in you that has never reached the surface in a relationship — a forgiveness, a confession, an encouragement you keep meaning to give. Bring it out this week, all the way to spoken words.

practices.title: TRACE A DESIRE UPSTREAM
practices.body: When a right desire rises in you this week — to pray, to apologize, to give — stop and name where it came from. God works the willing before He works the working. You will start noticing His fingerprints in places you had been crediting to your own discipline.

practices.title: TAKE A MURMUR FAST
practices.body: Go one full day with no commentary, spoken or internal, about a person or circumstance you did not choose. Note the hour you fail and what you were about to say. Gongysmos was the wilderness generation’s sin, and it is still the redeemed community’s most characteristic one.

practices.title: POUR SOMETHING OUT UNTRACEABLY
practices.body: Do one thing this week that will be entirely absorbed into someone else’s life — no credit, no record, no way to trace it back. Then test your gladness about it honestly. That is the libation, and Paul found joy in it while contemplating his own execution.

title: God Who Works in You
subtitle: from dust to the willing and the working
keyVerse: For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure.

passage.text: So then, my beloved, even as you have always obeyed, not only in my presence, but now much more in my absence, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling.
For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure.
Do all things without complaining and arguing,
that you may become blameless and harmless, children of God without defect in the middle of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you are seen as lights in the world,
holding up the word of life, that I may have something to boast in the day of Christ, that I didn’t run in vain nor labor in vain.
Yes, and if I am poured out on the sacrifice and service of your faith, I rejoice, and rejoice with you all.
In the same way, you also rejoice, and rejoice with me.

stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land first, then answer honestly.
lifeIntro: This week is about getting out of whichever ditch you are in — the grinding one or the waiting one — by taking the whole of verse thirteen instead of half of it.
lifePulls: A star does not strain to be visible. It is what it is, set where it was set, and the darkness does the rest.
prayer: Father, I keep choosing a ditch. Some weeks I grind as though it all depends on me. Some weeks I wait as though nothing is asked. You are working in me, both to will and to work, for Your good pleasure. Be upstream of what I want today. Stop the murmur in my mouth before it reaches my family. Then let me work hard and gladly, because You were at it before I woke. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, I keep choosing a ditch.
Some weeks I grind as though it all depends on me.
Some weeks I wait as though nothing is asked.
You are working in me, both to will and to work, for Your good pleasure.
Be upstream of what I want today.
Stop the murmur in my mouth before it reaches my family.
Then let me work hard and gladly, because You were at it before I woke.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure. God’s working is not the alternative to your effort; it is the ground of it, and He is upstream even of your wanting. Where that is true the murmur stops, and a man shines like a light set in a dark sky.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, off the two ditches you have been climbing between and onto the God who is working inside you while you read this. You have been in one of them. Either you have been grinding — carrying your sanctification like a man carrying a piano up stairs, alone, and privately certain that when you finally drop it everything will be over — or you have been waiting, told that striving is legalism, watching your sins take out long-term leases while you called it rest.

Lift up your eyes and see that both ditches are made from the same mistake. Both assume that if God is working, you are not, and that if you are working, God is not. Paul writes one sentence that will not permit it. Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling — for it is God who works in you. Not but. For. His working is why yours is worth beginning.

Lift up your eyes to how deep His working goes. Not merely the strength for the task; the wanting. He is upstream of your desires, in the room before you got there, producing the very willingness you thought you had manufactured on a good morning. Which means your best intentions were never yours to sustain, and your worst weeks were never yours to salvage.

Lift up your eyes to why He is doing it: for his good pleasure. Not as a duty accepted. As a delight determined upon. The God who is working in you is enjoying the work — and a craftsman who delights in what he is making does not abandon it because the material is difficult.
Lift your eyes off the ground you have been clinging to. Work today, hard and gladly, because Someone else has already been at it since before you woke.
closingVerse: For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure.
carry: Which half of Paul’s sentence have you been living in — and what would change today if you believed the God who commands the working is the one doing it?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: A man reaches a certain age and begins, without announcing it, to conserve.

It is not cowardice and he would resent the word. It is the accumulated wisdom of someone who has been burned — who gave himself to a church that did not appreciate it, poured years into a business partner who walked, carried a friend who never carried him back. He has learned. He still serves, but he serves with a governor on the engine. He gives, but he calculates first whether it will be received.
And he calls this maturity, because it does look like maturity. The reckless generosity of a younger man was partly naivety, and some of what he now withholds, he withholds for good reasons.

The dust does not tell you to stop serving. It tells you to meter it — to keep something in reserve, to make sure the expenditure is warranted before you make it, and above all never to spend yourself on something that might not work out. Under that arithmetic a man’s life slowly contracts to the size of what he is confident of recovering. Psalm 119:25 is the prayer of a soul that has been conserving for years and has quietly gone dry: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word (NKJV).

And the reviving word of Philippians 2 is a sentence Paul writes about two ordinary men who were not conserving anything. For they all seek their own, not the things of Jesus Christ — that is his survey of the available help. And against it he sets Timothy, who genuinely cared, and Epaphroditus, who nearly died carrying a bag of money across a sea.

sections.heading: Two Men and a Postal Service
pulls: The dust says meter it — never spend yourself on something you may not recover. Philippians 2 says the mind of Christ shows up as men who did not hold back.
paras: It would be easy to treat this passage as travel arrangements. Paul has just finished the highest Christology in his letters, and now he spends twelve verses discussing who is coming to visit and when.

But that is the point, and if you skip it you will miss the way Paul thinks. The hymn of chapter two is not a flight of theology that lands nowhere. It lands here, on two men. The mind of Christ — who did not grasp, who emptied Himself, who took the form of a servant — is not an abstraction Paul admires. It is a shape he can point to in people he knows by name.

Look at the pattern he sets up. Christ did not consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but poured Himself out. Timothy does not seek his own, but genuinely cares for others. Epaphroditus does not preserve his own life, but hazards it. It is the same movement three times, descending from the eternal Son to a young minister to a courier from a small church.

That descending line is how the gospel actually travels. It does not stay at the level of doctrine. It works its way down into the character of ordinary men until you can recognize the Christ of verse six in the conduct of a man carrying a satchel.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: THEY ALL SEEK THEIR OWN
paras: For I have no one else like-minded, who will truly care about you. For they all seek their own, not the things of Jesus Christ.

That is one of the loneliest sentences Paul ever wrote, and it is worth refusing to soften it. He is in custody. He has people around him — chapter one mentioned brothers who had grown bold, and chapter four will send greetings from saints in Caesar’s household. He is not alone in the room.

He is alone in this: when he looks for someone he can send on a long, thankless trip to care for a church that is not his own, the field narrows to one young man. Notice what Paul says is missing in the others. Not competence. Not orthodoxy. Not even zeal — the men in chapter one who preached out of selfish ambition were working hard. What is missing is that they seek their own. Their default setting, when a decision arrives, is their own interest, and no amount of activity changes which way the needle points at rest.

And notice the alternative he names: the things of Jesus Christ. Paul does not divide the world into selfish men and selfless men. He divides it by what a man is seeking. The opposite of self-interest is not having no interests. It is having Christ’s.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: A SON WITH HIS FATHER
paras: But you know the proof of him, that as a child serves a father, so he served with me in furtherance of the Good News.

Paul’s commendation of Timothy is not a list of accomplishments. It is a relationship and a track record. You know the proof of him — the Philippians had watched Timothy work, probably on the visit when the church was founded, and the evidence was in.

And the image is domestic. As a child serves a father. Paul does not say Timothy served him like a son serves a father — he says Timothy served with him, side by side, the way a boy works alongside his father in the family trade. That is a picture of apprenticeship rather than subordination: two men on the same job, one of them learning.

Which tells you how Christian character is actually transmitted. Not primarily by instruction. Timothy did not acquire this from a lecture; he acquired it by spending years next to a man who had it, doing the same work, watching what he did when the news was bad. If you want men who do not seek their own, you will not get them by teaching about it. You will get them by letting them work beside someone who does not.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: THE MAN WHO WAS HOMESICK AND ASHAMED
paras: Then comes Epaphroditus, and his story is more human than you may remember. He was sent from Philippi with a financial gift for Paul — a long, expensive trip undertaken on behalf of a poor church. Somewhere in it, or upon arrival, he fell seriously ill. Paul is blunt about how serious: he was sick, nearly to death.

And what troubles Epaphroditus is not his own condition. Since he longed for you all, and was very troubled because you had heard that he was sick. Word had gotten back to Philippi, and Epaphroditus is in distress because his home church is worried about him. He is lying near death and his anxiety is about their anxiety. He may also have carried something heavier — the sense that he had been sent to do a job and had instead become a burden.

Then Paul says something that should permanently change how you talk about God’s mercy in illness: but God had mercy on him, and not on him only, but on me also, that I might not have sorrow on sorrow.

Read that carefully. Paul — the apostle who could say that to die is gain — admits that this man’s death would have laid a grief on him he did not want to carry on top of the grief he already had. He does not spiritualize it. He does not say he would have rejoiced in God’s sovereign plan, though he believed in it entirely. He says it would have been sorrow upon sorrow, and he calls the recovery mercy.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: HOLD SUCH PEOPLE IN HONOR
paras: Receive him therefore in the Lord with all joy, and hold such people in honor, because for the work of Christ he came near to death, risking his life to supply that which was lacking in your service toward me.

Paul is sending a man home who may be arriving under a cloud. He left with a commission and he is coming back early, having been ill, without having completed the term of service the church probably intended. There would have been people in Philippi ready to think less of him.

So Paul gets ahead of it, and he does it with a rare word. Risking his life translates a verb that means to expose oneself to danger, to hazard one’s life — to put it where it may be lost. Epaphroditus did not carefully calculate an acceptable level of exposure. He put his life down as the stake, and he nearly lost it.

And Paul’s instruction is not sympathy. It is honor. Hold such people in honor — the word means valued, precious, held at a high price. The church is to receive him not as a man who failed to finish but as a man who spent himself to the edge, and to treat that as the standard of what is honorable among them.

Which is the quiet correction in the whole passage. Every church honors something; the only question is what. Philippi is told to honor a man whose great achievement was that he did not hold back — and in so doing, to honor in an ordinary courier the same mind that was in Christ Jesus.

stations.verse: For I have no one else like-minded, who will truly care about you.
stations.question: Is there anyone whose interests I carry as if they were my own?
stations.gloss: equal-souled; one whose inner life matches
body: another’s PHILIPPIANS 2:20 — THE ONLY OCCURRENCE IN THE NEW TESTAMENT Isopsychos joins isos, equal, to psychē, soul. It appears only here in the New Testament. The Greek Old Testament uses the same word in Psalm 55:13 for a companion so close he is described as a man’s own equal — his familiar friend. Paul is not saying Timothy agreed with him. Agreement is cheap and he had plenty of it. He is saying Timothy’s inner life ran on the same current — that when Paul cared about the Philippians, Timothy cared about them too, without being asked, and at the same depth.

And the second half of the verse gives the evidence: who will truly care about you. The verb is the ordinary word for anxious concern, the same root Paul will forbid in chapter four when it is turned inward. Turned inward it is the anxiety a believer is told to hand over. Turned outward on other people, it is the mark of a soul that has been made like somebody else’s.
stations.live: Name one person whose good you carry without being asked. If you cannot name one, that is the assignment — pick someone this week and start carrying it.

stations.verse: But you know the proof of him, that as a child serves a father, so he served with me in furtherance of the Good News.
stations.question: What in me has actually been tested and proven?
stations.gloss: proven character; the quality left in a thing after it has been
body: tested PHILIPPIANS 2:22; ROMANS 5:4; 2 CORINTHIANS 2:9 Dokimē comes from dokimazō, to test metal by fire to establish whether it is genuine. The noun does not name the test; it names the result — the proven quality that remains once the assaying is done. Romans puts it in a chain: suffering produces perseverance, and perseverance produces dokimē.

So Paul’s commendation of Timothy is not a character reference. It is an assay report. You know the proof of him — the Philippians had watched this young man under load and the metal had come out clean.

And note how the proof was acquired: as a child serves a father, so he served with me. Not under Paul but alongside him, the way a boy works with his father in the family trade. That is how this kind of character moves from one man to another. Not by instruction — Timothy did not learn it in a classroom — but by years of standing next to someone under the same load and watching what he did when the news was bad.
stations.live: Find one younger believer and put them beside you in something real this week. Character transfers by proximity under load, not by advice.

stations.verse: since he longed for you all, and was very troubled because you had heard that he was sick.
stations.question: When I am suffering, whose distress am I actually thinking about?
stations.gloss: to be in anguish; distress that unsettles a man to his
body: depths PHILIPPIANS 2:26; MATTHEW 26:37; MARK 14:33 Adēmoneō is a rare and heavy word. Its derivation is uncertain, but its use is not: it describes distress that goes past worry into anguish — a man not at home in himself. In the New Testament it appears only three times, and two of them are in Gethsemane, where Jesus began to be sorrowful and severely troubled.

That is the word Paul selects for Epaphroditus. And the cause of the anguish is the surprising part. He is lying near death in a foreign city, and what is tearing at him is that the people back home have heard he is ill and are worried about him.

He may also have been carrying something heavier and more familiar: he was sent to do a job and had become a burden instead. Men who spend themselves often end up needing care, and the needing is harder for them than the spending. Paul answers it by refusing to let the church treat it as failure.
stations.live: If you are the one currently needing care, stop apologizing for it this week. Being carried is part of the same fellowship as carrying.

stations.verse: Receive him therefore in the Lord with all joy, and hold such people in honor,
stations.question: Whom do I actually treat as honorable?
stations.gloss: held at a high price; precious, valued, honored
body: Entimos joins en, in, to timē, price or honor — literally, in the price range, and so valuable, held dear. Luke uses it of a centurion’s servant who was precious to him, and of the place of honor at a banquet. Peter uses it twice of Christ Himself, the living stone chosen by God, precious.

That is strong vocabulary for a sick courier from a poor church. Paul is not asking Philippi to be nice to a man who tried. He is telling them to assign a high price to him — to treat him as valuable in the way they would treat a person of standing.

And the timing is the pastoral genius of it. Epaphroditus is coming home early, ill, without having served out the term his church likely intended. There were people ready to think less of him. Paul gets ahead of the gossip and tells them exactly what to honor: not achievement, not completion, but a man who spent himself to the edge.
stations.live: Publicly honor one person this week whose service has gone unnoticed or been quietly discounted. Say specifically what they spent and what it cost them.

stations.verse: because for the work of Christ he came near to death, risking his life to supply that which was lacking in your service toward me.
stations.question: What have I been holding in reserve because I am not confident of getting it back?
stations.gloss: to hazard one’s life; to expose oneself
body: to danger PHILIPPIANS 2:30 — THE ONLY OCCURRENCE IN THE NEW TESTAMENT Paraboleuomai is related to paraballomai, to expose oneself. It means to hazard, to risk one’s life where it can genuinely be lost. It occurs only here in the New Testament.
The word does not soften the risk. It means exposure that is real — a life put where it could be taken, with no guarantee of getting it back.

That is the word Paul uses of an ordinary man carrying a bag of money across a sea. Epaphroditus did not compute an acceptable level of exposure. He put his life down as the stake and nearly lost it — for the work of Christ. And Paul’s response is not to caution the church against recklessness. It is to tell them that this is what honor looks like.
stations.live: Identify one thing you have been metering because you might not recover it — time, money, affection, reputation. Put it on the table this week.

practices.title: FIND THE GOVERNOR
practices.body: Name the thing you have been metering because you are not confident of getting it back: hours, money, affection, the benefit of the doubt. Write down what happened that taught you to conserve it. Then decide whether that lesson has become wisdom or just a smaller life.

practices.title: CARRY SOMEBODY’S INTEREST
practices.body: Name one person whose good you carry without being asked, at the depth you carry your own. If you cannot name one, that is the week’s work — pick someone and begin. Isopsychos is not agreement. It is a soul running on the same current as another.

practices.title: PUT SOMEBODY BESIDE YOU
practices.body: Take a younger believer and bring them into something real this week — a hard conversation, a difficult job, a visit nobody wants to make. Timothy did not learn this in a lecture. He learned it standing next to a man under load, watching what he did when the news was bad.

practices.title: HONOR THE UNNOTICED
practices.body: Publicly honor one person whose service has been discounted. Say specifically what they spent and what it cost them. Paul got ahead of the gossip about Epaphroditus by telling the church exactly what to value, and a congregation becomes whatever it decides to honor.

practices.title: STAKE ONE THING
practices.body: Put something on the table this week where it can genuinely be lost — a conversation that may not go well, a gift you will not see the use of, an offer of help that may be refused. Paraboleuomai is a gambler’s word, and Paul used it as praise.

title: Men Who Spend Themselves
subtitle: from dust to a life poured out
keyVerse: because for the work of Christ he came near to death, risking his life to supply that which was lacking in your service toward me.

passage.text: But I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you soon, that I also may be cheered up when I know how you are doing.
For I have no one else like-minded, who will truly care about you.
For they all seek their own, not the things of Jesus Christ.
But you know the proof of him, that as a child serves a father, so he served with me in furtherance of the Good News.
Therefore I hope to send him at once, as soon as I see how it will go with me.
But I trust in the Lord that I myself also will come shortly.
But I counted it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus, my brother, fellow worker, fellow soldier, and your apostle and servant of my need,
since he longed for you all, and was very troubled because you had heard that he was sick.
For indeed he was sick, nearly to death, but God had mercy on him, and not on him only, but on me also, that I might not have sorrow on sorrow.
I have sent him therefore the more diligently, that when you see him again, you may rejoice, and that I may be the less sorrowful.
Receive him therefore in the Lord with all joy, and hold such people in honor,
because for the work of Christ he came near to death, risking his life to supply that which was lacking in your service toward me.

stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land first, then answer honestly.
lifeIntro: This week is about finding the governor you have quietly installed on your own generosity, and removing it in one specific place.
lifePulls: Every church honors something. The only question is what — and Philippi was told to honor a man whose achievement was that he did not hold back.
prayer: Father, I have been seeking my own and calling it wisdom. I have metered my love because I was not sure I would get it back. Your Son did not hold back, and You ask no more of me than He gave. Give me the care Timothy had for people who were not his own. Give me the nerve Epaphroditus had to put my life where it could be lost. Put someone in front of me today who cannot repay the outlay. And teach me to honor the men who spend themselves. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, I have been seeking my own and calling it wisdom.
I have metered my love because I was not sure I would get it back.
Your Son did not hold back, and You ask no more of me than He gave.
Give me the care Timothy had for people who were not his own.
Give me the nerve Epaphroditus had to put my life where it could be lost.
Put someone in front of me today who cannot repay the outlay.
And teach me to honor the men who spend themselves.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: Paul follows the hymn of Christ’s descent with travel plans, and that is where the hymn lands: Timothy, who truly cared, and Epaphroditus, who risked his life for the work of Christ. The dust tells a burned man to meter himself and calls it maturity. The mind of Christ shows up in men who did not hold back, and the church is told to honor them.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, off the reserve you have been protecting and onto the Man who kept nothing back. You did not become careful all at once. It happened in increments, each one reasonable — the church that did not appreciate what you gave, the friend who did not carry you in return, the years you poured into something that came to nothing. And every one of those taught you a small lesson in conservation until your life had contracted to the size of what you were confident of recovering.

Lift up your eyes to the One you are following. He was existing in the form of God and did not consider it a thing to be clutched. He emptied Himself. He took a servant’s form, a man’s body, and a criminal’s death, and at no point did He compute an acceptable level of exposure. There was never a moment when Christ decided to hold something back in case it was not appreciated.

Lift up your eyes to what that mind produced in ordinary men. Timothy, who cared about a church in another country as if it were his own. Epaphroditus, who took a bag of money across a sea and put his life on the table for it, and nearly lost. Neither of them was an apostle. Both of them had the same mind, and you can see it in the way they spent.

Lift up your eyes, and stop protecting the reserve. You are not being asked for more than He gave, and you are not being asked to give from a supply that runs out — He works the willing and the working in you, for His own good pleasure, and He has never yet run a man dry who was spending at His direction.
Lift your eyes off the ground you have been clinging to, and put something on the table.
closingVerse: because for the work of Christ he came near to death, risking his life to supply that which was lacking in your service toward me.
carry: What have you been holding in reserve because you might not get it back — and what did it cost the One who held back nothing?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Every man who has been in church a long time has built something, and most of the time he does not know it is there.

It is not a list he would recite. It is more like a general sense of where he stands — accumulated out of years of attendance, a marriage he did not walk out of, kids he raised in the faith, money given, positions held, sins he has never committed and looks down on slightly. He would deny all of it under direct questioning. He knows the doctrine. He would tell you plainly that he is saved by grace alone.

But watch him after a bad month, and watch him after a good one, and you will see the file open. When his week has gone well, he prays with a certain ease. When it has gone badly, he approaches God the way a man approaches a creditor. Something is being consulted, and it is not the cross.

The dust does not ask you to deny justification by faith; that would be too obvious and you would catch it. It simply lets you keep a second account open — a quiet supplemental record of your own decency — and lets you draw on it when you need to feel secure. The account never gets audited because you never admit it exists. Psalm 119:25 is the prayer of a soul that has been living off the wrong balance: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word (NKJV).
And the reviving word of Philippians 3 is a man opening his own portfolio in public — a religious résumé few men could match — and writing the entire thing off as a loss.

sections.heading: Paul Opens His Books
pulls: The dust never asks you to deny justification by faith. It just lets you keep a second account open, and lets you draw on it when you need to feel secure.
paras: Notice first what provokes this. Chapter three opens with a swerve. Paul has been saying farewell, sending greetings, wrapping up — Finally, my brothers, rejoice in the Lord! — and then, abruptly, the tone hardens: Beware of the dogs; beware of the evil workers; beware of the false circumcision.

The same men who wrecked Galatia were circling Philippi. And Paul, who had told the Galatians he wished they would cut themselves off, is no gentler here. He calls them dogs — the word Jews used of Gentiles, now aimed back at Jewish teachers. He calls their rite a mutilation. He is not losing his temper; he is refusing to let a polite word be used for a thing that damns.

Then he does something he almost never does. He produces his credentials. Not because he values them — he is about to destroy them — but because he wants to be sure nobody can say he despises what he never had. If any other man thinks that he has confidence in the flesh, I yet more.

And he lists it: circumcised the eighth day, not a proselyte but a native son. Of the stock of Israel. Of the tribe of Benjamin, which gave Israel her first king and held Jerusalem. A Hebrew of Hebrews, keeping the language and the customs in a Greek world. A Pharisee, the strictest party. Zealous to the point of persecution. And as to the righteousness which is in the law — found blameless.
Seven items. Four of them he was born with, three of them he achieved. It is the strongest portfolio any man in that world could assemble, and he assembled all of it.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: WE ARE THE CIRCUMCISION
paras: Before the list, Paul makes a claim that would have sounded outrageous: For we are the circumcision, who worship God in the Spirit, and rejoice in Christ Jesus, and have no confidence in the flesh.

He is not saying the church has replaced Israel by displacing her. He is saying what the prophets said — that the true covenant people were always identified by a circumcised heart rather than a circumcised body, and that in Christ the reality has arrived. Moses had told Israel to circumcise the foreskin of their hearts. Jeremiah warned that the whole house of Israel was uncircumcised in heart. Paul is not innovating; he is reading his Bible.

And notice the three marks he gives of the real thing, because they are a useful diagnostic. They worship God in the Spirit — the service is Spirit-enabled, not flesh-managed. They rejoice in Christ Jesus — their boasting has an object outside themselves. And they have no confidence in the flesh — the file is closed.

Take the third one seriously. Paul does not say they have reduced their confidence in the flesh, or keep it in proper proportion. No confidence. Not as a backup, not as a supplement, not as a comfort on a good week.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: MOVING ENTRIES BETWEEN COLUMNS
paras: However, I consider those things that were gain to me as a loss for Christ.

Read the bookkeeping carefully, because Paul is precise. He does not say his advantages were worthless. He says they were gain — real assets, correctly valued at the time. What happened was not a revaluation of the items. It was the arrival of something that changed what counts as profit.

And the verb is the same one he used in chapter one, I consider — a deliberate reckoning, not a feeling. Paul made a decision about his ledger and he did not make it once. The tense shifts in the next verse to the present: I count all things to be a loss. He decided it on the Damascus road and he keeps deciding it, because the old entries do not stay written off by themselves.

Then he goes further than you may be willing to follow: and count them nothing but refuse, that I may gain Christ. The word is deliberately coarse. Paul is not saying his pedigree is now of secondary importance. He is saying it belongs in the place you throw things that are actively unpleasant to keep.

And the reason is never contempt for the things themselves. It is the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus, my Lord. A man does not write off good assets because he has grown cynical. He writes them off because something has arrived beside which they do not register.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: A RIGHTEOUSNESS NOT MY OWN
paras: Then comes the verse the Reformation was fought over, and Paul states it with surgical care.
And be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own, that which is of the law, but that which is through faith in Christ, the righteousness which is from God by faith.

Two righteousnesses are set against each other and they are mutually exclusive. The first is my own — Paul’s word is the possessive, and the source is named: of the law. It is the righteousness a man produces by doing. Paul had gone as far down that road as anyone in history and had been found blameless, and he still calls it his own and refuses it.

The second is from God — the preposition is one of origin, out of God. It comes through faith in Christ, which means faith is the instrument that receives it, not the achievement that earns it. Faith is empty hands.

And look at where it is located: be found in him. Not righteousness handed to a man standing at a distance, but righteousness that belongs to a man because he is inside Another. On the last day, when Paul is found, he intends to be found somewhere — and the somewhere is Christ, wearing a righteousness that was never generated in him.

That is the difference between a religion of achievement and the gospel, and it cannot be split. Either the righteousness that secures you originates in you and is validated by God, or it originates in God and is received by you. Paul had tried the first one with more success than you or I will ever have, and he threw it out.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: THAT I MAY KNOW HIM
paras: Then the aim of the whole exchange: that I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings, becoming conformed to his death, if by any means I may attain to the resurrection from the dead.

The man who wrote that had been a Christian for roughly a quarter century. He had seen the risen Christ, been caught up to the third heaven, planted churches across two continents, and written much of what the church now calls the New Testament. And what he wants is to know him.

Notice the order of the three things. First the power of His resurrection — the life that raised Christ operating in a man now. Then the fellowship of His sufferings — not admiration of the cross from a distance but partnership in it. Then becoming conformed to his death, an ongoing process by which a believer’s life takes the shape of a crucifixion.

You would have arranged it as suffering first, then power, with the power as the reward. Paul puts resurrection power first, because the power is what makes the fellowship of suffering survivable. You do not endure your way to resurrection life. You are given resurrection life and it enables you to endure.

And the last clause — if by any means I may attain — is not doubt about whether he will make it. It is the language of a man reaching, straining, with everything on one outcome. He has written off the portfolio. There is nothing behind him to fall back on. He has staked the whole thing on being found in Christ.

stations.verse: Beware of the dogs; beware of the evil workers; beware of the false circumcision.
stations.question: What religious requirement have I let someone attach to my standing with God?
stations.gloss: a mutilation; a cutting-down of the flesh
stations.xref: PHILIPPIANS 3:2 — THE ONLY OCCURRENCE IN THE NEW TESTAMENT
body: Katatomē joins kata, down, to temnō, to cut. It appears only here in the New Testament, and Paul turns it into a sarcastic wordplay: peritomē is circumcision, the covenant sign; katatomē is a mutilation, the kind of ritual gashing the law itself forbade to Israel because the pagan nations practiced it.

The point is savage and exact. A sign of the covenant, demanded as a condition of acceptance with God, stops being a sign of anything. It becomes a wound. Paul is not attacking circumcision; he had Timothy circumcised. He is attacking a rite that has been promoted into a requirement.

And there is a warning in it for people who no longer argue about circumcision. Any good practice can become a katatomē the moment it is presented as what completes you before God — a discipline, a translation, a schooling choice, a style of worship. Make it a condition and you have turned a sign into a cutting.
stations.live: Name the practice you have quietly made a condition of your standing with God. Keep the practice this week if it is good. Retire it as a condition.

stations.verse: However, I consider those things that were gain to me as a loss for Christ.
stations.question: What is on my list — the things that quietly make me feel acceptable?
stations.gloss: loss; damage sustained, the debit side of a transaction
body: Zēmia is the commercial opposite of kerdos, the gain Paul spoke of in chapter one. It means loss, forfeit, damage — what a merchant writes in the column that hurts. Luke uses it twice in the shipwreck narrative, of cargo thrown overboard and a voyage that cost more than it earned.

That shipwreck image is worth holding. When a ship is going down, the sailors do not throw the cargo over because it is worthless. They throw it over because it is heavy, and because staying afloat has become the only thing that counts. Paul is not sneering at his pedigree. He is jettisoning it.

And he keeps the accounting honest. He does not say those things were always loss; he says they were gain to me — real assets, correctly valued at the time. What changed is not the items but the arrival of something beside which they do not register. Conversion was, for Paul, an accounting change he has never reversed.
stations.live: Write your own list — the seven things that quietly make you feel acceptable. Do not moralize about them. Just write them, and then write loss across the page.

stations.verse: Yes most certainly, and I count all things to be a loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus, my Lord, for whom I suffered the loss of all things, and count them nothing but refuse, that I may gain Christ
stations.question: Would I be willing to say out loud what I actually think my religious record is worth?
stations.gloss: refuse; what is thrown out — table scraps, dung,
body: waste PHILIPPIANS 3:8 — THE ONLY OCCURRENCE IN THE NEW TESTAMENT Skybalon appears only here in the New Testament, and translators have been managing it for centuries. It covers everything discarded as worthless and offensive — the scraps swept from a table and thrown to dogs, and also excrement. Ancient writers used it for both. It is not a polite word, and Paul did not choose a polite word. The force is in the category, not merely the coarseness. Refuse is not a lesser good. It is not something you keep in a smaller place. It is what you put outside the house because it is actively unpleasant to have indoors.

And notice the target. Paul is not saying his heritage, his training, and his blameless record were bad things. He is saying that the moment any of them is held as a ground of standing before God, it becomes refuse — and that he had rather be found empty-handed in Christ than carry the finest portfolio in Judaism to the judgment seat.
stations.live: Take the item on your list you are proudest of. Say the sentence honestly this week: ‘As a reason for God to receive me, that is refuse.’ Notice how hard it is to say.

stations.verse: and be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own, that which is of the law, but that which is through faith in Christ, the righteousness which is from God by faith,
stations.question: Whose righteousness am I planning to be found in?
stations.gloss: righteousness; the standing of one who is right
body: before the bench PHILIPPIANS 3:9; ROMANS 1:17, 3:21–22; 2 CORINTHIANS 5:21 Dikaiosynē belongs to the law court. It is the noun for the condition of a man against whom no charge stands — not a description of his temperament but of his status. Paul’s whole doctrine of justification runs on the distinction between having such a status and producing it.

And here he sets two of them side by side and makes them exclusive. One is my own — its source is named, of the law, and it is produced by doing. The other is from God, the preposition marking origin, and it is received through faith in Christ. Faith is not the achievement that earns it. Faith is the empty hand that takes it.

Then notice the location, which is the sweetest part of the verse: be found in him. Not a righteousness mailed to a man standing at a distance. On the last day Paul intends to be found inside Another, wearing a standing that was never generated in his own life. Second Corinthians states the exchange bluntly: For him who knew no sin he made to be sin on our behalf; so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.
stations.live: When you fail this week, do not go looking for your own righteousness. Say where you actually live: ‘I am found in Him, and the righteousness there is not mine.’

stations.verse: if by any means I may attain to the resurrection from the dead.
stations.question: Is the resurrection something I believe — or something I am reaching for?
stations.gloss: a rising out from among; resurrection out of
body: the dead PHILIPPIANS 3:11 — THE ONLY OCCURRENCE IN THE NEW TESTAMENT Exanastasis joins ek, out from, to anastasis, resurrection — and Paul then adds the preposition a second time in the phrase that follows, so the line reads, with deliberate awkwardness, the out-resurrection out from among the dead. He is piling up the prepositions on purpose. This is the only occurrence in the New Testament.

He is not describing resurrection in general; everyone is raised. He is describing being raised out from among the dead — the believer’s own rising, the one Christ’s rising guarantees, which the same letter will describe as a body of humiliation conformed to a body of glory.

And the tentative-sounding clause before it is not doubt. If by any means I may attain is the language of a man reaching with everything he has, and it follows directly on a paragraph in which he threw away every asset he owned. He has nothing behind him to fall back on. That is exactly why he is straining forward — a man with no reserves runs differently.
stations.live: Name one thing you have been treating as a fallback in case the Christian life does not work out. Let it go this week, and reach.

practices.title: WRITE THE LIST
practices.body: Paul named seven items — four he was born with, three he achieved. Write yours. Not the things you are proud of in general; the things that make you feel acceptable to God when your week has gone well. Be specific and do not moralize while you write.

practices.title: WRITE LOSS ACROSS IT
practices.body: Then take the item you are proudest of and say the sentence out loud: as a reason for God to receive me, that is refuse. Pay attention to how much resistance the sentence meets. The resistance is the measure of how much weight the item was carrying.

practices.title: FIND THE KATATOMĒ
practices.body: Name the good practice you have quietly promoted into a condition — a discipline, a schedule, a standard you hold. Keep the practice this week if it is genuinely good. Retire it as a condition, and notice whether you still want it once it is no longer buying anything.

practices.title: WATCH YOURSELF AFTER A BAD DAY
practices.body: Do not change anything on purpose. Just observe how you approach God on the evening of a day you are ashamed of, and compare it to a day you are pleased with. The difference between the two is the size of the account you say you do not have.

practices.title: AIM AT KNOWING HIM
practices.body: Paul, twenty-five years in, wanted one thing: that I may know him. Pick one habit this week — reading, prayer, the Lord’s table — and do it with that as the stated aim rather than improvement, insight, or discipline. Say it before you begin.

passage.text: Finally, my brothers, rejoice in the Lord! To write the same things to you, to me indeed is not tiresome, but for you it is safe.
Beware of the dogs; beware of the evil workers; beware of the false circumcision.
For we are the circumcision, who worship God in the Spirit, and rejoice in Christ Jesus, and have no confidence in the flesh;
though I myself might have confidence even in the flesh. If any other man thinks that he has confidence in the flesh, I yet more:
circumcised the eighth day, of the stock of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews; concerning the law, a Pharisee;
concerning zeal, persecuting the assembly; concerning the righteousness which is in the law, found blameless.
However, I consider those things that were gain to me as a loss for Christ.

Yes most certainly, and I count all things to be a loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus, my Lord, for whom I suffered the loss of all things, and count them nothing but refuse, that I may gain Christ
and be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own, that which is of the law, but that which is through faith in Christ, the righteousness which is from God by faith,
that I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings, becoming conformed to his death,
if by any means I may attain to the resurrection from the dead.

stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land first, then answer honestly.
lifeIntro: This week is about finding the second account you have been quietly keeping, and closing it.
lifePulls: Either the righteousness that secures you originates in you and is validated by God, or it originates in God and is received by you. Paul tried the first with more success than you will, and threw it out.
prayer: Father, I have no confidence in the flesh — not as a backup, not on a good week. I confess the second account I keep and draw on when I feel ashamed. Close it. Let me be found in Christ, wearing a righteousness I did not produce, the righteousness that comes from You by faith. I want to know Him, and the power of His resurrection. Let me carry nothing today that I have to defend. In Jesus’ name, amen.

bottomLine: Paul lays out a record few men could match and counts all of it loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus, his Lord. The dust lets you keep a second account open to draw on when you need to feel secure. Philippians 3 closes it: you are found in Him, not having a righteousness of your own, but the righteousness which is from God by faith.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, off the quiet second account you have been keeping and onto the righteousness that was never yours to produce. You would deny the account exists. You know the doctrine and you could teach it. But watch yourself on the evening of a day you are ashamed of, and watch yourself on the evening of a good one, and you will see a file being consulted that has no business being open. Lift up your eyes to the man who closed his. Paul had a portfolio you cannot match: born into the covenant, of Israel, of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews, a Pharisee, zealous past the point of violence, and — his own word — blameless as to the righteousness in the law. Whatever quiet advantage you are holding, he held a better one, and he did not misplace it or grow out of it. He threw it out, and he used a word for the throwing that decent men avoided.

Lift up your eyes and see why he did it. It was not disgust. He did it because something arrived beside which the whole portfolio failed to register. The excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus, my Lord. A man does not jettison good cargo out of cynicism. He jettisons it because staying afloat has become the only thing that counts.

Lift up your eyes and hear where Paul intends to be standing on the last day. Not beside his record. Found in him — inside Another, wearing a righteousness that came out of God and was received with empty hands, which is the only kind of hand that can receive anything.
Lift your eyes off the ground you have been clinging to. You have nothing God needs, and you are wearing everything He requires.
closingVerse: and be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own, that which is of the law, but that which is through faith in Christ, the righteousness which is from God by faith.
carry: What is in the second account you say you do not keep — and what would today feel like if the only righteousness you had were Christ’s?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: There are two ways a man’s past can keep him from moving, and they look nothing alike.

The first is the obvious one. He did something, or something was done to him, and it sits at the center of how he understands himself. He does not think about it constantly; he does not have to. It is a ceiling. Whatever he attempts, some part of him has already calculated that a man with his history does not get past a certain altitude, and the calculation runs quietly underneath every decision he makes.

The second is stranger and less often named. His past was good. There was a season when God used him, when the work was fruitful and he knew it, and he has been living off it ever since. He is not ashamed of anything. He is finished — comfortably, invisibly finished — because a man who believes he has already arrived has no reason to run.
The first man is haunted. The second is retired. And they are both standing in the same place, which is why Paul addresses them in one sentence.

The dust tells you the past is where the truth about you lives — either the failure that caps you or the success that excuses you — and either way it keeps your eyes pointed backward over your shoulder while your feet go nowhere. Psalm 119:25 is the prayer of a soul that has been looking the wrong direction for years: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word (NKJV).

And the reviving word of Philippians 3 is a man near the end of his life, with more behind him than you will ever have, saying plainly: not that I have already obtained, or am already made perfect; but I press on.

sections.heading: Not That I Have Already Obtained
pulls: The haunted man and the retired man are standing in the same place — one looking back at a failure, one looking back at a season. Paul addresses them in a single sentence.
paras: Consider who is saying it. Paul has been a Christian for about twenty-five years. He has planted churches on two continents, seen the risen Christ, been caught up into the third heaven, and written letters the church will read for two thousand years. He has just finished describing the deepest exchange in his theology.
And his own assessment of his progress is: not yet.

That single clause does more pastoral work than most sermons on assurance. If Paul had not arrived, then the standard you have been failing to meet is a standard nobody has met. The gap you feel between what you are and what you should be is not evidence that something has gone wrong in your case. It is the ordinary condition of every runner still on the track, including the fastest man in the field.

And notice that the admission does not paralyze him. He says not yet and then immediately says I press on. Those two belong together, and each one guards the other. Without not yet, a man stops running. Without I press on, a man lies down and calls it humility.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: TAKEN HOLD OF BEFORE HE TOOK HOLD
paras: But I press on, that I may take hold of that for which also I was taken hold of by Christ Jesus.

Everything in this passage rests on that sentence, and most readers run past the second half. Paul says he is straining to take hold — and then says he is only doing so because he was first taken hold of. The same verb, both directions. His pursuit is a response to a seizure.

Picture it honestly. On the Damascus road Paul was not seeking Christ; he was carrying warrants against His people. He did not take hold of anything. He was taken hold of — arrested, flattened, blinded, claimed — and everything he has done since has been a man running after the One who caught him.

Which is exactly how effort and grace fit together in the Christian life, and why the two ditches from Week Five keep collapsing here. Paul strains hard. He also knows that the straining is downstream of a grip that was laid on him before he had any interest in the race. He is not running to be caught. He is running because he was.
And there is a great mercy in the grammar. If your perseverance depended on your hold on Christ, it would be only as reliable as your worst month. Paul locates the security in the other hand.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: THE FORGETTING THAT FREES
paras: But one thing I do: forgetting the things which are behind, and stretching forward to the things which are before.

Be precise about what Paul means by forgetting, because he plainly does not mean amnesia. This is the man who told the Corinthians he was the least of the apostles because he persecuted the church, and told Timothy he was the chief of sinners. He never stopped naming his past out loud.

Biblical forgetting is not the erasure of memory. It is the refusal to let a thing govern. To forget, in this sense, is to strike an item from the list of things that determine what you do next. Paul remembers everything. He has simply removed all of it from the controls.

And he removes both kinds. The things which are behind covers the whole of it — the crimes and the achievements, the persecution and the church-planting. He will not be governed by his failures and he will not coast on his successes. Both are behind, and behind is not where a runner looks.

Then the posture: stretching forward. The verb pictures a sprinter at full extension — head down, torso out over the line, hand reaching past the body toward the tape. Everything in the runner is committed to what is ahead. There is not a part of him left over to glance backward with.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: ONE THING
paras: One thing I do. Three words in English, two in Greek, and they explain the entire man.
