Paul was not a simple person. He was a trained rabbi, a working tradesman, a strategist who planned missionary journeys across an empire, a writer, a fundraiser, and a pastor to churches across several provinces. His life had more moving parts than yours. And he says one thing.

This is not a call to have fewer responsibilities. It is a call to have one center. You are probably the reverse of Paul: your schedule is simpler than his and your heart is more divided. You are doing eight things, not because your duties require it but because you have never decided what the duties are for.

And the one thing is not a project. I press on toward the goal for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus. The goal is Christ. The prize is Christ. The calling is God’s and it is upward, and everything Paul does in a given week is a form of running toward one Person.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: THE MIND OF THE MATURE
paras: Then Paul does something almost playful. Let us therefore, as many as are perfect, think this way.

Two verses earlier he said he was not already made perfect. Now he addresses the perfect and includes himself. He is using the word in its two senses deliberately — not finished, and yet mature — and the joke has a point: the mark of a mature Christian is knowing he is not a finished one. Any man who thinks he has arrived has thereby proved he has not.

If in anything you think otherwise, God will also reveal that to you. That is a relaxed sentence from a man who has just been calling people dogs. Paul is not anxious about the ones who have not seen it yet. He trusts God to do the revealing, which is a good deal more patience than you likely extend to a brother who disagrees.
And then the closing instruction, which is the practical end of the whole chapter: Nevertheless, to the extent that we have already attained, let’s walk by the same rule. Let’s be of the same mind.

Do not wait for complete clarity before you obey. Walk in what you have. You are not standing still until the fog lifts; you are moving at the light you have been given, and the rest will be shown to a man in motion. That is how a church stays together while its members are at different places on the same road — not by pretending to identical maturity, but by walking in the same direction at the light each one has.

stations.verse: Not that I have already obtained, or am already made perfect; but I press on, that I may take hold of that for which also I was taken hold of by Christ Jesus.
stations.question: Is my security resting on my grip on Christ — or on His grip on me?
stations.gloss: to seize; to lay hold of and make one’s
body: own PHILIPPIANS 3:12–13; 1 CORINTHIANS 9:24; JOHN 1:5 Katalambanō intensifies lambanō, to take, with kata — to take down, to seize, to grasp firmly. Paul uses it in 1 Corinthians of a runner who does not merely enter the race but takes the prize. John uses it of darkness that could not overcome the light. Watch the double use in this verse. Paul presses on that I may take hold — and then names the reason: of that for which also I was taken hold of by Christ Jesus. The same verb in both directions, and the divine seizure comes first.

On the Damascus road Paul was not searching. He was carrying warrants. He did not lay hold of Christ; Christ laid hold of him — arrested, blinded, claimed — and every mile he has run since has been a response to a grip that was applied when he had no interest in the race. Which means his perseverance does not rest on the strength of his own hand. If it did, it would be only as reliable as his worst month.
stations.live: When your hold on Christ feels thin this week, do not try to tighten it. Say the better fact: ‘I was taken hold of, and that hand has not moved.’

stations.verse: Brothers, I don’t regard myself as yet having taken hold, but one thing I do: forgetting the things which are behind, and stretching forward to the things which are before,
stations.question: What is behind me that is still deciding what I attempt?
stations.gloss: to stretch out toward; to reach at full
body: extension PHILIPPIANS 3:13 — THE ONLY OCCURRENCE IN THE NEW TESTAMENT Epekteinomai stacks two prepositions on teinō, to stretch: epi, toward, and ek, out. It occurs only here in the New Testament, and the picture is athletic and precise — a sprinter at the tape, head down, torso out past his feet, hand reaching ahead of his own body.

Everything in such a runner is committed forward. There is no portion of him held in reserve and no part left over to glance backward with. That is the posture Paul claims for a man twenty-five years into the Christian life who has just admitted he has not arrived.

And notice what he pairs it with. The forgetting is not amnesia — this is the man who kept telling people he had persecuted the church. Biblical forgetting is the refusal to let a thing govern. He remembers everything and has taken all of it off the controls, the crimes and the achievements alike, because behind is not where a runner looks.
stations.live: Name the one thing behind you that is still setting your ceiling. Do not try to stop remembering it. Take it off the controls: ‘That is real, and it does not decide what I attempt.’

stations.verse: I press on toward the goal for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.
stations.question: If I had to name the one thing I am running toward, could I do it in a sentence?
stations.gloss: the mark; the point on which the eye is fixed
stations.xref: PHILIPPIANS 3:14 — THE ONLY OCCURRENCE IN THE NEW TESTAMENT
body: Skopos comes from skopeō, to look at intently — the root behind the English word scope. It names the mark on which the eye is fixed — the goal. It occurs only here in the New Testament.

The word carries its own discipline. A skopos is singular by definition; a man who is watching two points is not watching either. Which is why the verse before begins one thing I do — the goal is one because a goal can only ever be one.

And Paul’s life was not simple. He was a rabbi, a tentmaker, a strategist, a writer, a fundraiser, a pastor to many churches. He had more moving parts than you and fewer competing centers. You may be the reverse: a simpler schedule, a more divided heart, eight pursuits and no mark.
stations.live: Write the sentence: ‘The one thing I am running toward is ___.’ If the sentence takes more than one clause, you have found the problem.

stations.verse: I press on toward the goal for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.
stations.question: Am I running for a reward I could lose — or for One who cannot be taken?
stations.gloss: the victor’s prize, awarded by the judge of the games
body: Brabeion comes from brabeus, the judge who presided over the Greek games and awarded the crown. The word names the prize specifically as something conferred by an official at the end — not seized by the runner, but handed to him from the stand. That detail matters in a passage about straining. Paul runs with everything he has, and the prize is still given rather than taken. The brabeus decides, and the runner receives. The same man who wrote about empty hands in verse nine has not quietly refilled them here.

And notice what the prize is. Not a crown described separately from Christ. The prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus — the calling is upward, the caller is God, and the content of the whole thing is the Person Paul has already said he counts everything else as refuse to gain. He is not running toward a reward Christ hands out. He is running toward Christ.
stations.live: Name the reward you are actually working for this year. Hold it beside Paul’s and ask honestly which one could be taken from you by a bad decade.

stations.verse: Let us therefore, as many as are perfect, think this way. If in anything you think otherwise, God will also reveal that to you.
stations.question: Where have I quietly concluded that I have arrived?
stations.gloss: complete; brought to the end intended for it, hence mature
body: Teleios comes from telos, an end or goal. It does not mean flawless; it means having reached the intended completion — a grown man as against a child, fruit that is ripe rather than green. Hebrews uses it of believers who are past milk and able to take solid food.

Paul is playing with the word, and the play is the point. Two verses earlier he said he was not already made perfect — the verb from this same root. Now he addresses as many as are perfect and includes himself. Not finished, and yet mature.

The joke carries the lesson. The mark of a teleios Christian is precisely that he knows he is not a finished one; any man who thinks he has arrived has proved by the thinking that he has not. And Paul is unbothered by those who have not yet seen it: God will also reveal that to you. He does not argue them into maturity. He trusts God to do the revealing and tells everyone to keep walking at the light they have.
stations.live: Find the area where you have stopped expecting to grow. Ask God this week to reveal what you cannot currently see there — and then walk at the light you already have.

practices.title: NAME YOUR CEILING
practices.body: Write down the thing behind you that is still deciding what you attempt. Do not try to stop remembering it; that is not what Paul means. Write beside it: this is real, and it does not set my altitude. Take it off the controls, not out of your memory.

practices.title: CHECK FOR RETIREMENT
practices.body: Now the other direction. Is there a season of fruitfulness you have been living off? A time when God used you that has quietly become your evidence instead of your history? A retired man and a haunted man are standing in the same place, both facing backward.

practices.title: WRITE THE ONE SENTENCE
practices.body: Finish it: the one thing I am running toward is ___. If it takes more than one clause, you have found the trouble. Paul’s life had more moving parts than yours and fewer centers.

practices.title: REST ON THE OTHER HAND
practices.body: When your grip on Christ feels thin this week — and it will — do not try to tighten it. Say the better fact aloud: I was taken hold of. Your perseverance does not rest on the strength of your hand. It rests on a grip that was laid on you before you had any interest in the race.

practices.title: WALK AT THE LIGHT YOU HAVE
practices.body: Identify one thing you already know to do and have been deferring until you feel clearer about it. Do it this week anyway. Paul’s instruction is to walk by what you have attained and let God reveal the rest — and God reveals things to men who are already moving.

title: One Thing I Do
subtitle: from dust to a forgetting that frees
keyVerse: Brothers, I don’t regard myself as yet having taken hold, but one thing I do: forgetting the things which are behind, and stretching forward to the things which are before, I press on toward the goal for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.

passage.text: Not that I have already obtained, or am already made perfect; but I press on, that I may take hold of that for which also I was taken hold of by Christ Jesus.
Brothers, I don’t regard myself as yet having taken hold, but one thing I do: forgetting the things which are behind, and stretching forward to the things which are before,
I press on toward the goal for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.
Let us therefore, as many as are perfect, think this way. If in anything you think otherwise, God will also reveal that to you.
Nevertheless, to the extent that we have already attained, let’s walk by the same rule. Let’s be of the same mind.

stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land first, then answer honestly.
lifeIntro: This week is about turning around — getting your eyes off what is behind you, whether it shames you or satisfies you, and putting them on one mark.
lifePulls: Biblical forgetting is not amnesia. Paul remembered everything. He had simply taken all of it off the controls.
prayer: Father, You took hold of me before I was looking for You. I was going the wrong way, and You laid hold of me anyway. I have been running with my head turned toward what is behind. Take my failures off the controls, and my good seasons too. Let there be one thing, one goal, and let it be Christ. Keep me walking by the light I have, and show me the rest as I go. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, You took hold of me before I was looking for You.
I was going the wrong way, and You laid hold of me anyway.
I have been running with my head turned toward what is behind.
Take my failures off the controls, and my good seasons too.
Let there be one thing, one goal, and let it be Christ.
Keep me walking by the light I have, and show me the rest as I go.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: Paul says he has not yet arrived, and he says he presses on, and both are true at once. He reaches forward only because he was first taken hold of by Christ Jesus. So forget what is behind — not by erasing it, but by taking it off the controls — and press on toward the goal.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, off the ground behind you and onto the One who is ahead. You have been running with your head turned. Perhaps it is the thing you did, sitting in the middle of your self-understanding like a stone, quietly calculating for you what a man with your history is permitted to attempt. Or perhaps it is the good season — the years when God plainly used you — and you have been living off it long enough that you have stopped expecting anything new.
Either way your feet have gone slow, because nobody runs well looking over his shoulder.

Lift up your eyes to a man who had more behind him than you will ever have. Paul had crimes he never stopped naming and successes the church still reads about, and he said one thing I do: forgetting the things which are behind. Not erasing. He remembered every bit of it. He had simply taken all of it off the controls, so that nothing in his history got a vote on what he did next.

Lift up your eyes and see why he can run like that. He is not straining to be caught. I press on, that I may take hold of that for which also I was taken hold of by Christ Jesus. The grip came first. On a road where you were going the wrong direction with warrants in your hand, Someone laid hold of you — and your security has never once depended on the steadiness of your own fingers.
Lift your eyes off the ground you have been clinging to. There is one mark, and He is at the end of it, and He has had hold of you the whole way.
closingVerse: Brothers, I don’t regard myself as yet having taken hold, but one thing I do: forgetting the things which are behind, and stretching forward to the things which are before, I press on toward the goal for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.
carry: What is behind you that still gets a vote on what you attempt — and what would this week look like if you took it off the controls without pretending to forget it?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: A man does not usually decide to become worldly. He settles.

It happens across a decade and nothing marks the transition. He still believes what he believed. He still goes. But somewhere along the line his imagination stopped reaching past the visible, and now his hopes, his fears, and his calculations are all conducted entirely at ground level. Retirement is the horizon. The body is the problem. The house, the health, the kids’ trajectory, the account balance — these are the things that can actually make a week good or bad, and he would be embarrassed to admit how completely they do.
He has not stopped believing in heaven. He has stopped expecting it, which is a different thing and much harder to notice.

And there is a specific pressure that produces this. Bodies age. A man in his fifties is negotiating with a frame that no longer does what it did, and the negotiation is daily and undignified. The natural response is to divide: keep the faith for the soul and make private peace with a body that is simply losing. He stops praying about it. He assumes the decline is outside the reach of the gospel.

The dust tells you that the visible world is the real one and the invisible world is the hoped-for one, and that maturity consists in adjusting your expectations to what you can see. Psalm 119:25 is the prayer of a soul that has been lowering its eyes for years: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word (NKJV).

And the reviving word of Philippians 3 is that your commonwealth is somewhere else, that a Savior is coming from there, and that the very body you have made peace with losing is the thing He is coming to transform.

sections.heading: Weeping While He Writes
pulls: He has not stopped believing in heaven. He has stopped expecting it, which is a different thing and much harder to notice.
paras: Notice the emotional temperature of this passage, because it is easy to miss.
For many walk, of whom I told you often, and now tell you even weeping, as the enemies of the cross of Christ.
Paul is crying. Not raising his voice — weeping, and he says he has told them about these people repeatedly. Whoever they are, he knows them, and the knowing is what makes it unbearable.

Who were they? Paul does not identify them precisely, and the description fits more than one group. Whose god is the belly may mean the food laws, or it may mean simple appetite. Whose glory is in their shame may refer to circumcision, or to sins openly celebrated. What is certain is that they were inside the orbit of the church — you do not weep over strangers, and you do not warn a congregation about people they will never encounter.

And observe the charge: not enemies of Christ, but enemies of the cross of Christ. That is a narrower and more disturbing accusation. A man can affirm Jesus and be at war with the cross — because the cross is where a man is told he brings nothing, where appetite is crucified, where glory is redefined as a public execution. The cross has always been the part that people work around.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: WATCH THE ONES WHO WALK
paras: Before the warning comes the alternative: Brothers, be imitators together of me, and note those who walk this way, even as you have us for an example.

It sounds presumptuous until you remember what Paul has just finished saying. Two paragraphs ago he told them he had not arrived. He is not offering himself as a finished product. He is offering himself as a man visibly running in a particular direction, and he is telling them to run the same way.

And the word for imitation here is a compound — imitate together. Not each man privately modeling himself on the apostle, but a congregation doing it as one body, which is a very different picture. This is corporate apprenticeship.

Then he widens it: note those who walk this way. Look around your own church and find the people whose lives have this shape. The verb means to mark, to observe attentively, to keep your eye on. You may never have done this deliberately. You take in teaching from people you will never meet and pay very little attention to the older believers three rows back whose walk you could actually watch over years. Paul assumes the Philippians have such people in front of them. So do you, and God put them there to be marked.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: THE MIND THAT SETTLED
paras: Whose end is destruction, whose god is the belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who think about earthly things.

Four clauses, and the last one is the diagnosis that produced the other three. The verb is phroneō — the same word that has been running through this letter since chapter two, where Paul told them to have this mind which was in Christ Jesus. It does not mean to think about occasionally. It means to have one’s mind set, to be oriented, to have settled one’s disposition in a direction.

These people have set their minds on earthly things. That is the root, and everything else grows from it. Make the visible world your frame of reference and appetite becomes god by default, because appetite is what the visible world runs on. Make the visible world your frame and shame becomes glory, because there is no higher court to appeal to.

And notice that the sin Paul names is not an action. It is an orientation. That should trouble comfortable men more than a list of vices would, because a man can be free of every item on a vice list and still have a mind that has completely settled at ground level. You will not catch this by auditing your behavior. You catch it by noticing what your daydreams are made of and what your anxieties are about.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: A COLONY OF HEAVEN
paras: For our citizenship is in heaven, from where we also wait for a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ.

The word is politeuma — the noun matching the verb Paul used in chapter one. It means a commonwealth, a state, the body politic to which one belongs. And in Philippi, of all cities, the metaphor landed with force.

Philippi was a Roman colony. Its people held a citizenship whose capital most of them had never seen, and they understood perfectly what it meant to belong to somewhere else while living here. A colony was not an outpost of people longing to go home. It was Rome, planted — the life of the capital being conducted in a distant place.

That is the picture Paul hands them, and it corrects two errors at once. It corrects the man who has settled into the visible world, because his commonwealth is elsewhere and his conduct should show it. And it corrects the man who treats heaven as an escape hatch, because a colonist does not spend his years waiting to be evacuated. He represents.

And notice what they wait for. Not a place — a Person. From where we also wait for a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ. The verb is intense, used of eager and patient expectation. Every title in that phrase was claimed by Caesar. Savior. Lord. And the emperor’s own household, Paul will say a few verses later, has people in it who have transferred their allegiance.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: THE BODY OF OUR HUMILIATION
paras: Then the sentence this entire letter has been building toward: who will change the body of our humiliation to be conformed to the body of his glory, according to the working by which he is able even to subject all things to himself.

Go back to chapter two and look at the word. He humbled himself — tapeinoō, He made Himself low. Here is the noun from the same root: the body of our humiliation, tapeinōsis, the lowness you are actually in. Paul has deliberately used the same vocabulary at both ends of his letter, and the arc is the whole gospel in two words. He entered your tapeinōsis. He will end it.

And be clear about what He transforms. Not your soul only — your body, the specific frame you have made private peace with losing. The one that aches, that has a diagnosis attached to it, that will eventually stop. That body is not a write-off God intends to abandon and replace. It is the object of the verb. It will be conformed to the body of his glory — the same resurrection body Christ has now, the pattern already existing and already occupied.

Then the guarantee: according to the working by which he is able even to subject all things to himself. Paul anchors the promise to the power that will subdue the universe. Whatever force is required to bring everything in creation under Christ is the force committed to the renovation of your body. He has the strength left over. So the dust does not get the last word on your frame. The One who stooped into dust will raise it — and He will raise it into the likeness of His own glory.

stations.verse: Brothers, be imitators together of me, and note those who walk this way, even as you have us for an example.
stations.question: Have I chosen on purpose whose walk I am watching?
stations.gloss: a fellow-imitator; one who copies a pattern
body: alongside others PHILIPPIANS 3:17 — THE ONLY OCCURRENCE IN THE NEW TESTAMENT Symmimētēs joins syn, together with, to mimētēs, an imitator — the root behind the English word mimic. It appears only here in the New Testament, and the syn is doing real work. Paul does not say imitate me; he says be imitators together of me.

That corporate framing matters. Christian formation was never designed as a private arrangement between one believer and one model. It is a congregation copying a pattern side by side, comparing notes, correcting each other’s drift, and noticing together what the pattern actually looks like when it is lived.

And Paul immediately widens the field: note those who walk this way. The verb means to mark, to fix the eye on and keep watching. He assumes his readers have such people in front of them. So do you — usually a few rows back, unremarkable, twenty years further down the road, and almost never watched on purpose.
stations.live: Pick one older believer in your own church whose walk you respect. Watch them deliberately this month, and find one way to get close enough to see how they actually live.

stations.verse: For many walk, of whom I told you often, and now tell you even weeping, as the enemies of the cross of Christ,
stations.question: Where am I comfortable with Christ but quietly working around His cross?
stations.gloss: an enemy; one standing in active hostility
body: Echthros is not the word for a rival or an opponent in debate. It means an enemy — one in a posture of hostility. Paul uses it in Romans of what believers were before Christ reconciled them, and in 1 Corinthians of death itself, the last enemy that will be abolished.

And notice exactly what these people are said to be enemies of. Not of Christ — of the cross of Christ. That is narrower and more searching. A man can hold a high view of Jesus and be at war with the particular thing the cross does to him: it tells him he contributes nothing, it puts his appetites to death, and it redefines glory as a public execution.

Which is why Paul is weeping rather than arguing. These are not outsiders; you do not warn a congregation about people they will never meet. They are near enough to be known, orthodox enough to pass, and they have found a way to keep the Savior while working around His cross.
stations.live: Name the part of the cross you keep at arm’s length — the contributing nothing, the dying to an appetite, the shame. Bring that one part into your prayers this week by name.

stations.verse: whose end is destruction, whose god is the belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who think about earthly things.
stations.question: What do my daydreams and my anxieties tell me my mind is actually set on?
stations.gloss: to set the mind; to have a settled orientation
body: Phroneō is not the word for thinking a thought. It means to have one’s mind set — a disposition, an orientation, the direction a man’s inner life faces when nothing is demanding his attention. Paul uses it repeatedly in this letter, most famously in chapter two: Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus.

So the climactic charge against these men is not an act. It is a direction: who think about earthly things — whose minds have settled at ground level. And the three clauses before it are the consequences. Make the visible world your frame of reference and appetite becomes god by default, because appetite is the currency the visible world trades in. Make it your frame and shame becomes glory, because there is no higher court to appeal to.

That should unsettle respectable men more than a list of vices would. You can be clear of every item on a vice list and still have a mind that has completely settled downward — and you will not catch it by auditing behavior. You catch it by noticing what your daydreams are made of.
stations.live: For three days, note what your mind goes to when nothing is demanding it. Do not judge the entries. Just read the list at the end and see which direction it faces.

stations.verse: For our citizenship is in heaven, from where we also wait for a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ,
stations.question: Am I living as an expatriate waiting to go home — or as a colonist representing a capital?
stations.gloss: a commonwealth; the state in which one holds
body: citizenship PHILIPPIANS 3:20 — THE ONLY OCCURRENCE IN THE NEW TESTAMENT Politeuma is the noun matching the verb Paul used back in chapter one. It appears only here in the New Testament and means the body politic itself — the state, the commonwealth, the register in which a man’s name is kept.

Philippi would have felt it. The city was a Roman colony, its citizens enrolled in a capital far across the sea. And a colony is not a camp of exiles waiting for evacuation. It is the capital planted — the life of the home country being carried on at a distance.

That corrects two errors at once. It answers the man who has settled into the visible world, because his register is kept somewhere else. And it answers the man who treats heaven as an escape hatch, because colonists do not spend their years waiting to be extracted. They represent. And every title in the phrase that follows — Savior, Lord — was one Caesar claimed for himself.
stations.live: Before one ordinary appointment this week, say it plainly: ‘I am here as a citizen of somewhere else.’ Then conduct the meeting like a man representing a capital.

stations.verse: who will change the body of our humiliation to be conformed to the body of his glory, according to the working by which he is able even to subject all things to himself.
stations.question: Have I quietly written off my body as outside the reach of the gospel?
stations.gloss: lowness; the humiliated state of something
body: brought down PHILIPPIANS 3:21; LUKE 1:48; ACTS 8:33; JAMES 1:10 Tapeinōsis is the noun from tapeinoō, the verb in chapter two: he humbled himself. Mary uses it of her own low estate, which God regarded. Luke quotes Isaiah with it of the Servant whose justice was taken away in his humiliation.

Paul has chosen his vocabulary deliberately, and the arc of the whole letter is in these two words. In chapter two the Son tapeinoō — He made Himself low, all the way to the death of the cross. Here in chapter three the believer’s body is the soma of tapeinōsis — the frame you are actually in, aging, failing, undignified.

He entered your lowness. He will end it. And note precisely what gets transformed: not the soul only, but the body — the one with a diagnosis attached, the one you have made private peace with losing. It will be conformed to the body of His glory, a pattern that already exists and is already occupied. And the power pledged to the work is the power that will subject all things to Himself. He has strength to spare.
stations.live: Take the specific thing your body can no longer do. Say the promise over it once this week, out loud, with the body in view: ‘He will change this.’

practices.title: READ YOUR DAYDREAMS
practices.body: For three days, note where your mind goes when nothing is demanding it, and what your anxieties are about. Do not judge the entries as you write them. Read the list at the end of the third day and ask which direction it faces. Phroneō is not a thought; it is an orientation.

practices.title: MARK SOMEONE
practices.body: Pick one older believer in your own congregation whose walk you respect, and start watching on purpose. Then find a way to get close enough to see how they actually live. You take in teaching from people you will never meet and ignore the pattern God set three rows back.

practices.title: NAME THE PART YOU WORK AROUND
practices.body: The charge is enmity against the cross, not against Christ. Identify the part of the cross you keep at a distance — contributing nothing, the death of a particular appetite, the shame of it. Bring that specific part into your prayer this week by name.

practices.title: WALK IN AS A CITIZEN
practices.body: Before one ordinary appointment — a meeting, a difficult call, a family dinner — say it plainly to yourself: I am here as a citizen of somewhere else. Then conduct it that way. A colony is not a camp of people waiting to be evacuated. It is the capital, planted.

practices.title: SPEAK TO YOUR BODY
practices.body: Take the thing your body no longer does — the knee, the memory, the stamina, the diagnosis. Say the promise over it once this week with the body actually in view: He will change this. Not replace it and forget it. Change it, and conform it to the body of His glory.

title: Our Citizenship Is in Heaven
subtitle: from dust to the body of His glory
keyVerse: For our citizenship is in heaven, from where we also wait for a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will change the body of our humiliation to be conformed to the body of his glory.

passage.text: Brothers, be imitators together of me, and note those who walk this way, even as you have us for an example.
For many walk, of whom I told you often, and now tell you even weeping, as the enemies of the cross of Christ,
whose end is destruction, whose god is the belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who think about earthly things.
For our citizenship is in heaven, from where we also wait for a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ,
who will change the body of our humiliation to be conformed to the body of his glory, according to the working by which he is able even to subject all things to himself.

stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land first, then answer honestly.
lifeIntro: This week is about raising your eyes off ground level, and about refusing to write off the part of you that has been quietly excluded from your hope.
lifePulls: He entered your lowness. He will end it — and the body He transforms is the one you have already made private peace with losing.
prayer: Father, my mind has settled at ground level. I believe in heaven, but I have stopped expecting it. Turn my whole orientation upward, not just my attention. I am waiting for a Savior from there, the Lord Jesus Christ. He will change this body of humiliation to be like the body of His glory, and I give back to You the parts of it I had quietly given up on. Let me live today as a citizen of somewhere else. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, my mind has settled at ground level.
I believe in heaven, but I have stopped expecting it.
Turn my whole orientation upward, not just my attention.
I am waiting for a Savior from there, the Lord Jesus Christ.
He will change this body of humiliation to be like the body of His glory,
and I give back to You the parts of it I had quietly given up on.
Let me live today as a citizen of somewhere else.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: Paul weeps over men whose god is the belly and who think about earthly things. Against them he sets a citizenship in heaven, from where you wait for a Savior who will change the body of your humiliation to be conformed to the body of his glory. He entered your lowness, and He will end it.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, off the ground your imagination has settled on and onto the country whose register holds your name. You did not decide to become earthbound. You settled, over years, without a single moment you could point to — and now your hopes and your fears are conducted entirely at eye level, and heaven is something you believe rather than something you expect.

And you have quietly signed away the part that hurts most. The body. The frame that no longer does what it did, the diagnosis you have stopped praying about, the slow negotiation that occupies more of your attention than you admit. You have made peace with losing it, and you have called that maturity.

Lift up your eyes and read the promise again, with your own body in the room. A Savior who will change the body of our humiliation to be conformed to the body of his glory. Not your soul extracted from a ruin. This body — the object of the verb — transformed into the likeness of the body He is wearing right now.

Lift up your eyes and see the word He chose. In chapter two the Son humbled Himself, tapeinoō, all the way down to a criminal’s death. In chapter three yours is the body of tapeinōsis — the same root, the low place you are actually in. He went down into it on purpose, and He is coming back to raise it, by the same power that will one day bring the whole universe under His feet. He is not working at the limit of His strength on you.
Lift your eyes off the ground you have been clinging to. Your citizenship is elsewhere, your Savior is coming from there, and even your dust is on the list of things He intends to glorify.
closingVerse: For our citizenship is in heaven, from where we also wait for a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will change the body of our humiliation to be conformed to the body of his glory.
carry: What have you written off as beyond the reach of the gospel — and what would change today if you believed He intends to glorify even that?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Most men do not describe themselves as anxious. They describe themselves as responsible, and the two are almost impossible to tell apart from the inside.

He is not panicking. He is thinking ahead. He runs the scenarios because someone has to, and if he stopped running them the family would be exposed. He wakes at three and reviews the same five items, and by four he has not solved any of them and has simply rehearsed them in more detail. In the morning he will say he slept poorly. And the thing that keeps him doing it is a quiet conviction that the rehearsing helps — that vigilance is doing some of the work of provision, that a man who has thought hard enough about a danger has partly discharged his duty toward it. He has never said that out loud, because it would sound absurd. But it governs his nights. The dust does not tell you to worry. It tells you that your worry is a form of responsibility, and that the alternative to it is negligence. So a man who would never call himself fearful carries the weight of an outcome he cannot control, and calls the carrying love. Psalm 119:25 is the prayer of a soul that has been standing watch on a wall it was never posted to: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word (NKJV).

And the reviving word of Philippians 4 is that the wall is garrisoned by Someone else. In nothing be anxious — and then, instead of a technique, a transfer: tell God, and a peace you cannot produce or explain will take up the watch.

sections.heading: Two Women and a Whole Chapter
pulls: The dust does not tell you to worry. It tells you your worry is a form of responsibility — so a man carries an outcome he cannot control and calls the carrying love.
paras: Notice where the chapter starts, because the famous verses grow directly out of it. I exhort Euodia, and I exhort Syntyche, to think the same way in the Lord.

Two women, named in a letter the church has now read for two thousand years, because they could not get along. Paul does not describe the dispute; he plainly does not think the content is the issue. He repeats the verb — I exhort, I exhort — addressing each one separately, refusing to take a side or to treat one as the problem. And what he asks of them is phroneō again, the word that has run through the whole letter: to think the same way in the Lord. Not to reach agreement on the matter. To have the same mind — the mind of chapter two, the mind of the One who did not grasp.

Then he asks for help: I beg you also, true partner, help these women, for they labored with me in the Good News. These were not difficult peripheral people. They were co-laborers, women who had worked beside Paul in the founding of that church, whose names are in the book of life. Two genuinely converted, genuinely useful believers had gotten crosswise with each other, and it was disturbing a whole congregation.

That is the setting for everything that follows about rejoicing, gentleness, anxiety, and peace. Paul is not writing a devotional essay on worry. He is pastoring a church with a quarrel in it and a prison sentence hanging over its founder, and telling them where peace actually comes from.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: STAND FIRM IN THE LORD
paras: Therefore, my brothers, beloved and longed for, my joy and crown, stand firm in the Lord in this way, my beloved.

Count the affection in that sentence. Brothers. Beloved. Longed for. My joy. My crown. Beloved again. Six terms of endearment in a single verse, from a man in custody, aimed at people who are currently not getting along.

That is worth noticing before the correction comes. Paul establishes the affection first and does not ration it because of the quarrel. He is about to name two women publicly, and he wants the whole congregation to know exactly how he feels about them before he does it.

And the therefore reaches back to what he has just said. Because your citizenship is in heaven, because a Savior is coming from there, because the body of your humiliation will be transformed — therefore stand firm. The standing is grounded in the coming. A man holds a position because he knows what is on its way, not because he has calculated that he can hold it.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: REJOICE, AND THE LORD IS AT HAND
paras: Rejoice in the Lord always! Again I will say, “Rejoice!” Sixteen times in four chapters Paul uses the vocabulary of joy, and here he makes it an imperative and then repeats it in case it sounded optional. From a cell. To a divided church.

And the qualifier is the whole thing: in the Lord. Paul is not commanding an emotion to appear on demand, and he is not asking anyone to be pleased about their circumstances. He is commanding a direction. There is one object in which joy is always available because that object does not change with the news, and Paul has spent three chapters establishing who it is.
Then: Let your gentleness be known to all men. The Lord is at hand.

Those two sentences belong together and the second explains the first. Gentleness — the willingness not to press your rights all the way to the line — is nearly impossible for a man who believes that if he does not secure his own interests, nobody will. Which is precisely why Paul attaches the re-minder. The Lord is at hand. The Judge is near, both in presence and in coming. You can afford to be forbearing, because your case is not going unheard and you are not the one who has to enforce it.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: THE COMMAND NOT TO BE ANXIOUS
paras: In nothing be anxious.

Take the scope first. Not be anxious about less, not manage your anxiety, not be anxious only about things that warrant it. In nothing. And it is an imperative, which means anxiety is not merely a temperament to be accommodated but a disobedience to be repented of — a hard word until you see what Paul puts in its place.

Because he does not stop at prohibition, and a prohibition alone would be cruel. But in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God. Nothing and everything are set against each other deliberately. Nothing is left to worry about because everything has been given a place to go. Look at the three components. Prayer is the general word — the posture of address to God as God. Petition is deēsis, the asking that arises from a felt need, the same word from chapter one. And thanksgiving — which is the one you skip, and the one that does the most work. Gratitude forces a man to recall what God has already done, and a man remembering answered prayers asks differently than one who has forgotten them.

And notice the modest verb: let your requests be made known to God. Not resolved. Not surrendered with perfect trust. Made known. You are not required to pray well. You are required to say the thing out loud to the right Person.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: A PEACE THAT GARRISONS
paras: And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.

The verb behind guard is a military one: to garrison, to post a watch around a city — sentries on the wall, keeping the enemy out and the population in. Paul had used it before, in Galatians, of the law hemming men in until Christ came. Here the direction is reversed. The same encircling, but now it is peace that holds the wall. And notice what is being defended. Not your circumstances — Paul’s circumstances were a Roman prison and they did not improve. Your hearts and your thoughts: the affections and the reasoning, the two places where anxiety does its actual damage. God does not promise to garrison your situation. He promises to garrison you inside it.

Then the phrase that defines the peace: it surpasses all understanding. Not that it is unintelligible — that it exceeds. It rises above what the mind can produce or account for. It is not the peace of a man who has reasoned his way to calm, because such peace only lasts until the reasoning fails. This is a peace that arrives when the situation has not changed and does not justify it.

Which means the test of it is not whether you feel settled after you have solved the problem. The test is whether a peace you did not manufacture shows up on the wall while the problem is still standing there in front of you — and Paul writes it from a place where it did.

stations.verse: Therefore, my brothers, beloved and longed for, my joy and crown, stand firm in the Lord in this way, my beloved.
stations.question: Do the people I lead or love know how I feel about them before I correct them?
stations.gloss: the victor’s wreath, awarded at the end of the games
body: Stephanos is not the royal diadem. It is the woven wreath placed on the head of a winner at the games or on a guest of honor at a feast — the mark of a contest finished well. Paul uses it in 1 Thessalonians of his converts, asking what his crown of rejoicing will be at the coming of Christ, and answering: you.

So when he calls the Philippians my joy and crown, he is telling a divided congregation that they are what he intends to hold up on the last day. Not his letters. Not the churches planted or the miles traveled. People.

And mark where he puts it. He is one verse away from naming two quarreling women in a document the whole church will hear read aloud. He stacks six terms of affection in front of it — brothers, beloved, longed for, joy, crown, beloved again — and does not ration a single one because of the quarrel. Correction that arrives before affection rarely lands as correction. It lands as rejection.
stations.live: Before you correct anyone this week, say out loud what they are to you. Then correct. Watch what the order does to the conversation.

stations.verse: Rejoice in the Lord always! Again I will say, “Rejoice!
stations.question: Is my gladness currently sourced in something that can change by Friday?
stations.gloss: to rejoice; to be glad
body: Chairō is the ordinary Greek verb for gladness, and it shares a root with charis, grace — joy and grace are built on the same stem, which is no accident in Paul. It appears with its cognates some sixteen times in this short letter.

And every occurrence is from custody. He rejoices when rivals preach Christ to spite him. He rejoices at the prospect of being poured out like a drink offering. Now he makes it an imperative and, in case it sounded like a suggestion, repeats it.

The qualifier is what makes the command possible: in the Lord. Paul is not ordering an emotion to appear on demand and he is not asking anyone to be pleased about their circumstances. He is commanding a direction. There is exactly one object in which joy is always available, because that object does not move with the news — and he has spent three chapters establishing who it is.
stations.live: Each morning this week, before you check anything, name one thing that is true of Christ and will still be true on your worst day. Start there.

stations.verse: Let your gentleness be known to all men. The Lord is at hand.
stations.question: Where have I been insisting on a right that I could afford to let go?
stations.gloss: forbearing; not pressing one’s rights to the limit
body: Epieikēs is notoriously hard to render — translators have tried gentleness, moderation, reasonableness, forbearance, and none of them quite holds it. In Greek ethical writing it named the quality of a man who does not demand the last ounce the law allows him, who is willing to take less than his due for the sake of what is right. It is a strong man’s virtue, not a weak man’s. You cannot forbear a right you do not possess. Epieikēs describes someone with a legitimate claim who declines to press it all the way.

And Paul attaches a reason: The Lord is at hand. Those four words are the engine. A man will not stop enforcing his own case until he is certain someone else is hearing it — and the Judge is near, both present now and coming soon. You can afford to take less than you are owed, because the accounting is not finally in your hands and nothing is being lost that He has not recorded.
stations.live: Find the claim you have been pressing — in a negotiation, a family argument, an old grievance. Take less than you are owed this week, on purpose.

stations.verse: In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.
stations.question: Have I ever actually said to God the things I rehearse at three in the morning?
stations.gloss: a request; the specific thing asked for
body: Aitēma comes from aiteō, to ask. It does not name the act of praying; it names the content — the thing actually requested. Luke uses it of the crowd’s demand before Pilate, and John uses it of the petitions a believer has asked of God and knows he has. Which makes Paul’s command specific. In nothing be anxious, he says, and then he does not tell you to feel calmer. He tells you to name it. Let your requests be made known to God. Not a general unease handed upward in a sigh, but the actual items — the diagnosis, the son, the payroll, the conversation on Thursday.

And notice how little the verb asks. Made known. Not resolved, not surrendered with flawless trust. Made known — with thanksgiving, to a Father who already knows. You are not required to pray well. You are required to say the thing out loud to the right Person, and then the peace of God takes the watch.
stations.live: Write down the five things you rehearse at three in the morning. Say each one to God this week, by name, and add one sentence of thanks to each.

stations.verse: And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.
stations.question: Am I waiting for peace to follow a solution — or asking for a peace that arrives before one?
stations.gloss: to rise above; to surpass, to hold higher than
body: Hyperechō joins hyper, above, to echō, to have or hold — literally to hold above, and so to surpass or excel. Paul uses it three times in this letter and the three uses interpret each other. In chapter two the Philippians are to count others as hyperechō — above themselves. In chapter three the knowledge of Christ is surpassing, and everything else becomes refuse beside it. Here it is a peace that rises above all understanding. The word does not mean unintelligible. It means higher — above the level at which the mind operates. This is not the peace of a man who has reasoned his way to calm, because that peace lasts exactly as long as the reasoning holds. This is a peace that outranks the analysis.

And what it defends is not your circumstances. The verb Paul pairs with it is military — to garrison, to post sentries around a city. God does not promise to garrison your situation; Paul’s situation was a prison and it did not improve. He promises to post the watch around your hearts and your thoughts, the two places where anxiety does its actual damage, and to do it while the problem is still standing in front of you.
stations.live: Take the situation that has not changed. Ask specifically this week not for the solution but for the garrison: ‘Post the watch while this is still unresolved.’

practices.title: WRITE THE THREE A.M. LIST
practices.body: Put down the five things you rehearse in the dark. Do not solve them. Then say each one out loud to God this week, by name — because most of what passes for praying about a worry is simply worrying in His general direction without ever addressing Him.

practices.title: ADD THE THANKSGIVING
practices.body: To each item on that list, attach one sentence of thanks — something God has already done that bears on it. Gratitude is the component you skip, and it is the one that does the most work. A man remembering answered prayers asks differently than a man who has forgotten them.

practices.title: ASK FOR THE GARRISON, NOT THE SOLUTION
practices.body: Take the situation that is not changing. This week, stop asking primarily for the outcome and ask for the sentries: post the watch on my heart while this is still unresolved. Then notice whether something arrives that the circumstances do not account for.

practices.title: TAKE LESS THAN YOU ARE OWED
practices.body: Find the claim you have been pressing — in a negotiation, a family argument, an old grievance where you are genuinely in the right. Decline to press it all the way this week. You can afford it. The Lord is at hand, and the accounting is not finally yours to enforce.

practices.title: LEAD WITH AFFECTION
practices.body: Before you correct anyone this week — a child, an employee, a brother — say first what they are to you, and mean it. Paul stacked six terms of endearment in front of naming two quarreling women in public. Correction that arrives before affection is almost always heard as rejection.

title: The Peace That Stands Guard
subtitle: from dust to a garrisoned heart
keyVerse: In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.

passage.text: Therefore, my brothers, beloved and longed for, my joy and crown, stand firm in the Lord in this way, my beloved.
I exhort Euodia, and I exhort Syntyche, to think the same way in the Lord.
Yes, I beg you also, true partner, help these women, for they labored with me in the Good News with Clement also, and the rest of my fellow workers, whose names are in the book of life.
Rejoice in the Lord always! Again I will say, “Rejoice!”
Let your gentleness be known to all men. The Lord is at hand.
In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.
And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.

stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land first, then answer honestly.
lifeIntro: This week is about getting off a wall you were never posted to, and letting a peace you cannot manufacture take the watch.
lifePulls: God does not promise to garrison your situation. He promises to garrison you inside it — and Paul wrote that from a cell.
prayer: Father, here are the things I rehearse at three in the morning. I am not handing them over solved. I am making them known. I have called my worry responsibility. Forgive me. Thank You for what You have already carried for me this week. Make me gentle with the man I have been pressing, because You are near. Guard my heart and my thoughts in Christ Jesus before anything is resolved. Then let me sleep. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, here are the things I rehearse at three in the morning.
I am not handing them over solved. I am making them known.
I have called my worry responsibility. Forgive me.
Thank You for what You have already carried for me this week.
Make me gentle with the man I have been pressing, because You are near.
Guard my heart and my thoughts in Christ Jesus before anything is resolved.
Then let me sleep.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: Paul tells an anxious, divided church that the Lord is at hand, and then: in nothing be anxious, but let your requests be made known to God. Nothing is left to carry, because everything has somewhere to go. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, guards your heart and your thoughts in Christ Jesus while the problem is still standing in front of you.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, off the wall you have been pacing all night and onto the One who never asked you to stand that watch. You do not call it fear. You call it thinking ahead, running the scenarios, being the man who has considered what others have not. And underneath it runs a conviction you have never said aloud because it would sound ridiculous: that the rehearsing is doing something — that a danger sufficiently worried about has been partly handled.
It has not. You have spent years on a rampart nobody posted you to, and not one danger has been kept out by a single hour of it.

Lift up your eyes and hear the command, and hear that it comes with somewhere to put the weight. In nothing be anxious — and then, immediately, in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God. Nothing, because everything. Not one item left in your hands, because every item has been given an address. And notice how little is asked of your technique: made known. You are not required to pray beautifully or to feel settled while you do it. You are required to say the thing out loud to the right Person.

Lift up your eyes to what arrives next, which you did not manufacture. A peace that rises above your understanding — not beneath it, not instead of it, above it — and it does not wait for the situation to resolve. It takes the wall. Sentries around your heart and your thoughts, in Christ Jesus, while the problem is still standing there unchanged.
Lift your eyes off the ground you have been clinging to. The watch is kept. You are permitted to sleep.
closingVerse: In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.
carry: What have you been carrying because you believed the carrying was doing something — and what would tonight be like if you handed it over and let the garrison hold the wall?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Ask a man what would make him content and he will always have an answer, and the answer will always be a condition.

When the debt is paid. When this season at work is behind me. When the kids are settled. When the diagnosis comes back clear. When the house is finally sorted. He is not greedy; most of what he names is modest and reasonable. But notice the structure of every answer: contentment is downstream of a circumstance, and the circumstance has not arrived.

And here is the part he has not noticed. He has crossed this line before. Several of the conditions he once named have actually been met — the debt from ten years ago was paid, the season did end, the diagnosis was clear — and contentment did not arrive with them. A new condition simply took the old one’s place, quietly, without a moment of disappointment, because the mind generates the next one before the last one clears.

The dust tells you that contentment is a state produced by circumstances, so that a man who wants to be content must go and change his circumstances. Under that rule he will spend his whole life arranging conditions and will never once get there. Psalm 119:25 is the prayer of a soul that has been chasing a moving line for decades: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word (NKJV).

And the reviving word of Philippians 4 is a sentence from a man with no money and no freedom: I have learned in whatever state I am, to be content in it. Learned. Not discovered, not received in a moment — learned, the way a trade is learned, in conditions that were mostly bad.

sections.heading: A Verse Read Backwards
pulls: Paul is not saying Christ will help you accomplish anything you attempt. He is saying Christ will supply you in any condition you are put in — and he wrote it hungry.
paras: This week’s key verse is probably the most widely printed sentence Paul ever wrote, and it is almost always read backwards.
I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me.

It appears on locker-room walls, on the sleeves of athletes, in graduation cards and sales-team slide decks, and in every one of those settings it means something like this: with Christ’s help, I can accomplish whatever I set out to do. Aim high. He will supply the difference.

Read the paragraph it sits in and that meaning evaporates. Paul is not talking about achievement. He is talking about hunger. I know how to be humbled, and I also know how to abound. In everything and in all things I have learned the secret both to be filled and to be hungry, both to abound and to be in need. And then: I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me.

The all things is the list he just gave. Being full and being empty. Having plenty and having nothing. Abundance and need. Paul is not claiming Christ will help him accomplish anything he attempts; he is claiming Christ supplies him to endure any condition he is put in.

Which is a smaller promise and an infinitely better one. The slogan version fails the first time a man tries hard, prays hard, and does not get the outcome. Paul’s version holds in a prison cell, and it was written in one.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: THINK ABOUT THESE THINGS
paras: Before contentment comes a command about the mind, and the two are connected. Finally, brothers, whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report: if there is any virtue and if there is any praise, think about these things.

Six qualities and then a summary, and the verb at the end is logizomai — a bookkeeper’s word, to reckon, to take account of. Paul is not telling them to think positively. He is telling them to take deliberate account of a specific category of thing.

And it is a governed list, not a vague one. True, honorable, just, pure, lovely, of good report. These are not identical and the differences matter: a thing can be true and not lovely, honorable and not pure. Paul is asking for a mind trained to notice a whole range of goods and to dwell there on purpose.

Set this beside chapter three, where the enemies of the cross were defined by having their minds set on earthly things. The direction of a man’s mind has been Paul’s concern for two chapters now, and here he finally supplies the content. You do not defeat a downward orientation by resolving not to think about earthly things. You defeat it by giving the mind somewhere better to reckon.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: DO THESE THINGS
paras: The things which you learned, received, heard, and saw in me: do these things, and the God of peace will be with you.

Four verbs, and they describe a whole apprenticeship. Learned — instruction they received. Received — the technical word for a tradition handed over intact from one person to the next. Heard — what they were told about him when he was elsewhere. And saw in me — the part no book supplies.

Paul is not embarrassed to include the last one. He has already told them to be imitators together of him, and he knows that Christian living is transmitted as much by observation as by teaching. They watched how he handled money, opposition, illness, and a beating in their own city. That was curriculum.

Then the promise: and the God of peace will be with you. Compare it with the previous paragraph, where the peace of God garrisons the heart. Here it is not the peace but the God of peace, and He does not merely guard — He accompanies. Paul gives the gift in one verse and the Giver in the other, and the second is plainly the larger of the two.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: LEARNED, NOT NATIVE
paras: Not that I speak because of lack, for I have learned in whatever state I am, to be content in it.
The word behind content is autarkēs, and it is a loan from the philosophers, who used it for self-sufficiency — the condition of a man who needs nothing outside himself.

Paul takes the word and hollows out its center. He keeps the independence from circumstance and removes the self. His sufficiency is not in himself; two verses later he names its source, and it is a Person. What the philosopher sought by shrinking his desires, Paul receives by being supplied.

And note the verb twice over: I have learned. He says it again in the next verse — I have learned the secret. Contentment was not part of Paul’s natural equipment, and it did not arrive with his conversion. He acquired it, over years, in the only school that teaches it, which is a long sequence of conditions a man would not have chosen. That should be a relief to anyone who has been waiting to feel content. You are not lacking a temperament other Christians were issued. You are in the middle of a curriculum.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: INITIATED INTO A SECRET
paras: I know how to be humbled, and I also know how to abound. In everything and in all things I have learned the secret both to be filled and to be hungry, both to abound and to be in need.

Read the pairs and notice that both directions are named. You assume contentment is the skill of handling less. Paul lists abundance first and returns to it twice, because plenty is at least as hard. A man in need knows he is in trouble and prays accordingly. A man who has enough quietly stops.

And the verb behind learned the secret is a striking choice. It is the word used of initiation into the mystery religions — the rites in which a candidate was brought through stages and finally admitted to knowledge the uninitiated did not have. Paul borrows their vocabulary and applies it to something learned in a cell.

Then the summary line: I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me. The verb is endynamoō — not give strength to from outside, but to infuse power within. Christ does not stand beside Paul and help him lift. He is the strength in the lifting.

So the initiation is not into a technique. There is no method here, no discipline that produces contentment if practiced faithfully. The secret is a supply, and the supply is a Person, and what Paul learned over twenty years of hunger and plenty was simply how continuously available that Person is.

stations.verse: Finally, brothers, whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report: if there is any virtue and if there is any praise, think about these things.
stations.question: Would I defend what I have been feeding my mind if someone read the list back to me?
stations.gloss: honorable; carrying a dignity that commands respect
body: Semnos comes from sebomai, to revere or worship. In classical Greek it described what was august, weighty, worthy of reverence — used of gods, temples, and men of grave dignity. In the New Testament it appears only four times, three of them describing the character required of leaders and older men.

It is a hard quality to name in English. Honorable gets close; so does dignified, though that risks sounding stuffy. The idea is weight — the opposite of trivial, cheap, or frivolous. A semnos thing has substance enough to deserve respect.

And Paul places it second in a list of six that his readers are to reckon — logizomai, the bookkeeper’s word, to take deliberate account of. This is not positive thinking. It is a mind trained to notice a specific range of goods. Chapter three defined the enemies of the cross by their orientation downward; you do not fix a downward mind by resolving not to look down. You fix it by giving it something weightier to reckon.
stations.live: Take an honest inventory of what your mind has consumed in the last week. Replace one item with something semnos — something with actual weight to it.

stations.verse: The things which you learned, received, heard, and saw in me: do these things, and the God of peace will be with you.
stations.question: What have I received from others that I am supposed to be handing on intact?
stations.gloss: to receive something handed over; to take
body: delivery of a tradition PHILIPPIANS 4:9; 1 CORINTHIANS 11:23, 15:3; COLOSSIANS 2:6 Paralambanō joins para, from alongside, to lambanō, to take. It is the technical term for receiving a tradition transmitted from one person to another. Paul uses it in 1 Corinthians for the two most important deliveries in his ministry: the words of institution at the Lord’s Supper, and the gospel itself — I delivered to you first of all that which I also received.

So this is not casual learning. It is the language of a deposit changing hands without being altered in transit, and Paul places it in a chain of four verbs — learned, received, heard, saw — that together describe a complete apprenticeship.

Note the last of them especially: saw in me. Paul is unembarrassed to include his own conduct in the curriculum. The Philippians had watched him handle money, opposition, illness, and a public beating in their own city. Some things in the Christian life have never once been transmitted by instruction, and they are not the small things.
stations.live: Name one thing you received from an older believer that you have never passed on. Hand it to someone this week — in words, and then in something they can watch.

stations.verse: Not that I speak because of lack, for I have learned in whatever state I am, to be content in it.
stations.question: What condition am I currently waiting on before I expect to be content?
stations.gloss: sufficient in oneself; needing nothing from outside
body: the situation PHILIPPIANS 4:11 — THE ONLY OCCURRENCE IN THE NEW TESTAMENT Autarkēs joins autos, self, to arkeō, to be enough. Greek philosophy used it for self-sufficiency — the man who needs nothing outside himself.

Paul takes the word and removes its center. He keeps the independence from circumstance — that part he wants — and empties out the self. Two verses later he names where his sufficiency actually comes from, and it is not himself. What the philosopher sought by shrinking his wants, Paul received by being supplied.

And weigh the verb: I have learned. Contentment was not native to Paul and it did not arrive with his conversion. He acquired it over years, in the only school that teaches it — a long sequence of conditions he would not have chosen. If you have been waiting to feel content, you are not missing a temperament other Christians were issued. You are partway through a curriculum.
stations.live: Write down the condition you are waiting on. Then write down the one you were waiting on ten years ago, and ask what happened when it was met.

stations.verse: I know how to be humbled, and I also know how to abound. In everything and in all things I have learned the secret both to be filled and to be hungry, both to abound and to be in need.
stations.question: Which have I handled worse — having too little, or having enough?
stations.gloss: to initiate; to admit someone into knowledge held only by the
body: initiated PHILIPPIANS 4:12 — THE ONLY OCCURRENCE IN THE NEW TESTAMENT Myeō is related to the word behind English mystery. It belonged to the mystery religions — the rites in which a candidate was led through stages of preparation and finally admitted to knowledge the uninitiated did not possess. It occurs only here in the New Testament.

Paul borrows their vocabulary deliberately and relocates the initiation. The stages were not torchlit ceremonies. They were shipwrecks, beatings, hunger, and a prison cell, and the knowledge admitted to at the end was how to be content.

And notice the pairs, because both directions are named and abundance comes first. You assume contentment is the art of handling less. Paul knew better. A man in need knows he is in trouble and prays accordingly; a man who has enough quietly stops. Being filled is its own initiation, and you may have failed it without ever noticing there was a test.
stations.live: Ask which season damaged you more — the lean one or the comfortable one. Then name one specific way abundance has made you a worse pray-er.

stations.verse: I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me.
stations.question: Have I been using this verse to aim higher — when Paul wrote it about going hungry?
stations.gloss: to put power within; to infuse with strength from
body: inside PHILIPPIANS 4:13; EPHESIANS 6:10; 1 TIMOTHY 1:12; 2 TIMOTHY 4:17 Endynamoō joins en, in, to dynamis, power. The prefix is the whole point. It does not mean to give strength to someone from outside, the way a man braces a leaning wall. It means to put the power inside — to make strong from within.

So Christ is not standing beside Paul helping him lift. He is the strength in the lifting. And the grammar is a present participle: the One strengthening me, continuously, not a deposit made once and drawn down.

Now read the all things, because this is where the verse is most often taken from Paul. It is not a blank check for whatever a man attempts. It is the list in the verse before: filled and hungry, abounding and in need. Paul is claiming that Christ supplies him to endure any condition he is put in — which is a smaller promise than the poster version, and infinitely more durable. The slogan fails the first time a man tries hard and does not get the outcome. This one held in a cell.
stations.live: Apply the verse this week where Paul applied it — not to something you are attempting, but to something you are enduring. Say it over the condition you did not choose.

practices.title: NAME THE CONDITION
practices.body: Write down what you are currently waiting on before you expect to feel content. Then write the condition you were waiting on ten years ago. Note whether it was met, and note what happened to your contentment when it was. The line moves, and it moves silently.

practices.title: AUDIT THE DIET
practices.body: Take an honest inventory of what your mind has consumed in the past week — what you read, watched, scrolled, replayed. Do not moralize. Just read the list, and then replace one item with something semnos, something with actual weight to it.

practices.title: TEST THE HARDER DIRECTION
practices.body: Ask which season has damaged you more: the lean one or the comfortable one. Paul lists abundance first. A man in need prays; a man with enough quietly stops. Name one specific way having enough has made you a worse pray-er.

practices.title: HAND SOMETHING ON
practices.body: Name one thing you received from an older believer and have never passed along. Give it to someone this week — in words first, and then in something they can actually watch you do. Paul’s curriculum included saw in me, and that part cannot be taught any other way.

practices.title: APPLY THE VERSE CORRECTLY
practices.body: Take Philippians 4:13 and put it where Paul put it. Not on something you are attempting — on something you are enduring. Say it this week over the condition you did not choose and cannot change: I can do this through Christ, who is strengthening me.

title: I Have Learned to Be Content
subtitle: from dust to a strength poured in
keyVerse: I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me.

passage.text: Finally, brothers, whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report: if there is any virtue and if there is any praise, think about these things.
The things which you learned, received, heard, and saw in me: do these things, and the God of peace will be with you.
But I rejoice in the Lord greatly, that now at length you have revived your thought for me; in which you did indeed take thought, but you lacked opportunity.
Not that I speak because of lack, for I have learned in whatever state I am, to be content in it.
I know how to be humbled, and I also know how to abound. In everything and in all things I have learned the secret both to be filled and to be hungry, both to abound and to be in need.
I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me.

stationsIntro: Read each passage slowly, with your Bible open if you can. Let the verse land first, then answer honestly.
lifeIntro: This week is about noticing the moving line you have been chasing, and enrolling honestly in the school where contentment is actually taught.
lifePulls: What the philosopher sought by shrinking his desires, Paul received by being supplied. He kept the independence from circumstance and emptied out the self.
prayer: Father, I have been waiting on a condition before I let myself be content. Show me what it is, and take it off the throne. Christ is my sufficiency, in plenty and in want. Fill my mind with what is true, honorable, just, and pure. Put strength in me today for whatever I am given, not for whatever I want. Teach me the secret Paul learned, even if the school is hard. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, I have been waiting on a condition before I let myself be content.
Show me what it is, and take it off the throne.
Christ is my sufficiency, in plenty and in want.
Fill my mind with what is true, honorable, just, and pure.
Put strength in me today for whatever I am given, not for whatever I want.
Teach me the secret Paul learned, even if the school is hard.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: Paul learned to be content in whatever state he was in, and he learned it hungry as well as filled. The philosophers’ word for self-sufficiency is in his letter, with the self taken out and Christ put in. I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me is a promise for every condition you are put in, not a slogan for every goal you set.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, off the condition you have been waiting on and onto the One who has been sufficient the entire time you were waiting. You know the condition. It is specific, it is modest, and you could name it in four words. When this is behind me. When that is settled. And you have never noticed that you have stood at this line before and crossed it, and that contentment did not come across with you — a new condition simply took the old one’s place while you were not looking. Lift up your eyes and hear a man with no money, no freedom, and no verdict. I have learned in whatever state I am, to be content in it. Learned — which means he was not born with it and did not receive it at conversion. He acquired it, in the only school that teaches it, and the tuition was shipwrecks and beatings and an empty stomach.

Lift up your eyes to the sentence he ends on, and be careful with it, because the world has made a slogan of it. I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me is not a promise that you will accomplish what you set out to do. Read the verse before it. Filled and hungry. Abounding and in need.
